courses.title: Drinking water essentials
courses.description: Follow the journey from catchment to tap, understand treatment barriers and recognise evidence limits.

lessons.title: Source and hazards
points: Control health risks before water reaches consumers.
Catchment activities can introduce contamination.
Pathogens and dissolved chemicals may be invisible.
Disease-causing bacteria, viruses or protozoa.
Different barriers control different hazards and reduce dependence on one process.
lessons.intro: A drinking water supply begins in a catchment, not at the treatment plant. Activities around a river, reservoir or bore can change the hazards that operators must manage. Some changes are visible, while pathogens and dissolved contaminants may leave water looking clear. Thinking from source to consumer helps you connect each hazard with the barriers intended to control it and the evidence needed to show those barriers work.
lessons.example: After heavy rain, a rural intake still looks clear to the operator. A nearby livestock area has also flooded. Instead of treating appearance as proof of safety, the team checks the catchment information, source observations and relevant treatment records. The useful question is whether the changed conditions challenge the existing controls, rather than whether the water looks pleasant.

activity.prompt: Which observation most directly challenges an assumption that clear source water is safe?
options: The intake looks unchanged in a photograph.
Floodwater has reached an upstream livestock area.
The daily inspection sheet uses a new layout.
activity.feedback: The flooded livestock area introduces a plausible contamination pathway even when the intake looks clear. Appearance cannot establish the absence of pathogens or dissolved contaminants. Connect the changed catchment conditions to the supply risk assessment, relevant operational evidence and established response procedures before drawing a conclusion.

lessons.title: Treatment barriers
points: Destabilisation of fine particles so they can form removable flocs.
Gentle mixing that helps destabilised particles form larger flocs.
Particles that settle under the designed conditions.
Particles may pass through when performance deteriorates.
More light-scattering material that can affect treatment performance.
lessons.intro: Treatment is best understood as a sequence of barriers with different jobs. Coagulation helps destabilise fine particles, flocculation encourages larger flocs, and separation processes remove material under their designed conditions. These steps are related but are not interchangeable. A deterioration in one stage may affect what reaches the next, so following the water through the process is more useful than memorising equipment names alone.
lessons.example: A plant operator sees more particles in filtered water after a change in source conditions. The team traces the process backwards through filtration, settling and floc formation. They compare what each stage should accomplish with the recorded observations. This builds an investigation around barrier performance instead of assuming that a single final reading explains the whole problem.

activity.prompt: Why review upstream treatment when filtered water quality changes?
options: The filter is unaffected by the water entering it.
Every treatment step removes the same hazards.
Poor upstream particle removal can challenge a later barrier.
activity.feedback: A later barrier depends partly on the conditions delivered by earlier processes. Reviewing the treatment sequence helps locate possible causes and missing evidence. It does not by itself identify the failed component; operational records and the supply procedures are still needed to establish what happened and what response is appropriate.

lessons.title: Disinfection and performance
points: Delivered dose depends on validated operating conditions and water quality.
Operational evidence of disinfectant remaining in the water.
Adequate exposure under suitable conditions is needed for the target organisms.
No; dissolved nitrate needs a suitable separate treatment approach.
It can affect treatment chemistry and disinfection performance.
lessons.intro: Disinfection performance depends on conditions, not simply on whether a device is switched on. Relevant evidence can include water quality, operating conditions and the exposure delivered to the target organisms. A residual reading answers a particular operational question, while a different treatment process may be needed for a dissolved chemical. Keep the target hazard and the capability of the barrier together when interpreting any result.
lessons.example: A colleague suggests that a normal disinfectant residual proves a nitrate concern has been resolved. You separate two questions: what does the residual show about disinfection, and what evidence addresses the dissolved chemical? Reviewing the relevant treatment capability and laboratory information prevents a useful microbial control from being credited with removing a different type of hazard.

activity.prompt: What is the clearest response to the colleague’s nitrate conclusion?
options: A disinfectant residual does not establish nitrate removal.
Any normal operational reading proves every hazard is controlled.
Nitrate can be ignored when the water is disinfected.
activity.feedback: The residual is relevant evidence about a disinfectant remaining in the water, not proof of nitrate removal. Match each hazard to a process capable of controlling it. Review the appropriate analytical evidence and treatment information rather than extending one measurement beyond the question it can reasonably answer.

lessons.title: Distribution
points: Contaminant ingress where pathways exist.
Contamination can occur after treatment.
An actual or potential connection between drinking water and another system.
The time water spends within storage and distribution.
Conditions may differ across the distribution system.
lessons.intro: Water can become contaminated after it leaves treatment. Storage, pipework and connections create a distribution environment with its own vulnerabilities. Pressure changes, physical defects and cross-connections matter because they can create opportunities for ingress or reverse flow. Conditions also vary across the network. A result near the treatment plant may therefore tell a different story from evidence gathered at a distant consumer location.
lessons.example: The treatment outlet result is satisfactory, but a concern is reported at the far end of a network after a pressure interruption. The team reviews the affected area, storage and connections as well as treatment records. This avoids assuming that the outlet result describes every consumer’s water during an event occurring later in the supply chain.

activity.prompt: Which investigation best follows the source-to-consumer approach?
options: Repeat only the treatment outlet review and exclude the network.
Review the pressure event and affected distribution area alongside treatment evidence.
Assume distance from the plant makes the consumer report irrelevant.
activity.feedback: A distribution event can change water conditions after treatment. Bringing pressure history, local vulnerabilities and appropriately located evidence into the review addresses that possibility. The treatment outlet result remains useful, but its location and timing limit what it can establish about a separate part of the network.

lessons.title: Evidence and interpretation
points: Health-based maximum acceptable values for listed determinands.
Rules address monitoring and treatment assurance alongside the health limits.
Different units or reporting bases can change interpretation.
The sampled condition at that place and time within method limits.
Accreditation must cover the relevant test and context.
lessons.intro: Good evidence has a defined scope. A laboratory result describes a sample, method and reporting basis; an accreditation entry describes particular recognised activities. Drinking water limits and assurance rules also answer related but different questions. Before comparing a number with a requirement, check the determinand, units, expression basis, location and relevant context. This habit prevents confident decisions being built on measurements that do not actually match.
lessons.example: Two reports use similar labels for nitrate, but one reports nitrate and the other nitrate-nitrogen. A reviewer notices that the expression bases differ before comparing either with the selected requirement. The team obtains the relevant method and reporting information. The lesson is to establish a like-for-like comparison rather than treating similar words as identical evidence.

activity.prompt: What should happen before comparing the two nitrate results?
options: Select whichever number is smaller.
Treat the labels as interchangeable because both mention nitrate.
Confirm units and expression basis against the relevant requirement.
activity.feedback: Similar names can conceal different expression bases. Confirming units and basis is part of establishing whether a comparison is meaningful. Retain the original reports and any qualifications, and use a properly supported interpretation rather than silently changing labels or choosing the more reassuring number for the record.

lessons.title: Operational judgement
points: Follow the approved response procedure and investigate barrier performance.
Review the risk assessment and adequacy of controls.
Their locations and intended controls differ.
Measurements must remain reliable for operational decisions.
Record the uncertainty and seek the missing source-specific evidence.
lessons.intro: Operational judgement connects observations, uncertainty and agreed action. An unusual reading should lead to the established response process and a review of the evidence, rather than an improvised explanation. Reliable instruments, clear records and knowledge of the supply all matter. When evidence is missing, make that gap visible. Stating what remains uncertain is a practical decision skill, not a sign that the review has failed.
lessons.example: A sensor trend changes immediately after maintenance, while a field check is not yet available. The operator records the timing, checks the relevant maintenance and instrument information, and follows the site response procedure. The event is kept open until the missing evidence is resolved, rather than recording an unsupported statement that the new reading is definitely correct.

activity.prompt: Which note best supports the next operator’s decision?
options: Reading changed after maintenance; reliability check pending; response procedure followed.
Everything is normal because the equipment was recently serviced.
Delete the unusual values so the graph is easier to read.
activity.feedback: The first note preserves the observation, its context and the unresolved reliability question. That gives the next person something useful to investigate. Unsupported reassurance or deletion would hide uncertainty. Keep the record traceable and use the established escalation and response process while the evidence is checked.

courses.title: Sampling and laboratory evidence
courses.description: Plan representative samples, protect integrity and interpret results without losing traceability.

lessons.title: Plan before sampling
points: The monitoring purpose and the part of the supply being assessed.
Container and preservative requirements depend on the analysis.
Determinands, sites, timing, responsibility and relevant requirements.
Access, safe conditions, bottles, equipment and laboratory arrangements.
Supply characteristics and the applicable pathway affect what is required.
lessons.intro: A useful sample starts with a clear purpose. Source assessment, treatment assurance and distribution monitoring may require different locations, arrangements and interpretation. Planning brings the determinand, site, timing, responsibilities and laboratory instructions together before anyone collects water. It also exposes practical problems such as access or unavailable containers. A well-planned visit creates evidence that answers the intended question, rather than merely producing a laboratory number.
lessons.example: A collector is asked to obtain a sample for an unfamiliar analysis during a routine visit. Before leaving, they confirm the location, bottle requirements, receiving laboratory arrangements and purpose of the test. Discovering a special container requirement beforehand is easier to manage than finding out afterwards that an otherwise careful collection cannot support the intended analysis.

activity.prompt: What is the most useful first step for the unfamiliar test?
options: Use a spare bottle and let the laboratory decide later.
Confirm the purpose and laboratory collection requirements before sampling.
Collect from the easiest tap even if its location is different.
activity.feedback: Purpose and collection requirements determine whether the eventual result will be useful. Confirming these before the visit reduces avoidable gaps in container choice, location and delivery arrangements. Convenience alone does not establish sample suitability, and the laboratory cannot always repair problems introduced during planning or collection.

lessons.title: Collection integrity
points: Contact can contaminate the sample.
Follow laboratory instructions; rinsing can remove required preservative.
Prevent residual disinfectant continuing to act after collection.
Use an acceptable replacement and document any impact.
The procedure controls sampling contamination and matches the test purpose.
lessons.intro: Sample integrity depends on details that can seem minor in the field. Contact with a bottle opening, inappropriate rinsing or replacement of a specified container can change what reaches the laboratory. Preservatives and disinfectant neutralisers have particular purposes. Following the receiving laboratory’s instructions protects the connection between the sampled water and the reported result, while documenting any departure allows the result to be interpreted with its limitations visible.
lessons.example: A collector drops the cap of a microbiological bottle onto a dirty surface. They resist the temptation to wipe it and continue unnoticed. Instead, they use an acceptable replacement according to the collection arrangements and document the issue. The purpose is to avoid introducing handling contamination while retaining a clear account of what actually happened.

activity.prompt: Why is quietly wiping and reusing the dropped cap a weak response?
options: It may leave an unrecorded contamination risk in the sampling process.
The only concern is whether the outside label stays readable.
Any cap is acceptable if the sample is delivered quickly.
activity.feedback: The dropped cap creates uncertainty about collection integrity. An acceptable replacement and a record of the event preserve a stronger evidence trail. Fast delivery does not remove contamination introduced during handling, and an undocumented workaround prevents the laboratory or reviewer from considering a potentially important limitation.

lessons.title: Field observations
points: A sample identifier linked to site, date, time and collector.
They can help explain results and source conditions.
Some parameters can change after collection.
Retain the observation and investigate rather than invent a value.
An unreliable instrument can mislead sampling decisions.
lessons.intro: Field observations give a result its setting. A sample identifier, site, time and collector connect the bottle to the visit, while weather, source conditions and relevant field measurements may help explain unusual findings. Some conditions can change after collection. Record what was observed and distinguish it from what is unknown; an honest gap is more informative than a value supplied from memory or expectation.
lessons.example: During collection, an instrument will not stabilise, but the sample itself is obtained under the agreed procedure. The collector records the instrument issue and observed conditions without inventing a field value. A later reviewer can then separate the laboratory result from the missing measurement and decide what additional evidence is needed to interpret that visit.

activity.prompt: What should the field sheet show for the unreliable measurement?
options: The usual value from the previous visit.
An estimated value written as though it were measured.
The observation that a reliable value was not obtained, with context.
activity.feedback: Recording the missing reliable measurement makes the limitation clear. A previous or estimated value cannot stand in for an observation made during this visit. Keep the sample identity and other field information intact, then investigate the instrument and any consequences for interpretation through the appropriate procedures.

lessons.title: Transport and records
points: The method and the receiving laboratory's requirements.
Under the specified temperature, protection and delivery conditions.
Sample identity and transfers from collection to analysis.
Holding-time compliance, laboratory comments and result suitability.
Resolve and document the discrepancy before relying on the result.
lessons.intro: Transport is part of the sampling method rather than an administrative task added afterwards. Delivery conditions, holding times and identification records affect what the laboratory can reasonably report. Chain-of-custody information connects collection and subsequent transfers. When a discrepancy appears, investigate and document it before treating the result as straightforward evidence. A number without a reliable account of its sample can be difficult to use responsibly.
lessons.example: A laboratory reports that the sample label and submission form show different collection times. The reviewer returns to the original field record and speaks with the collector rather than choosing a convenient time. Once the discrepancy is resolved or clearly described, the laboratory can consider its significance alongside the relevant analysis and holding-time requirements.

activity.prompt: Which action best protects the evidence trail?
options: Resolve and document the timing discrepancy using the original records.
Change both times to the time the courier arrived.
Ignore the discrepancy because the result has already been issued.
activity.feedback: Original records provide the starting point for resolving inconsistent sample information. A documented correction or unresolved limitation supports transparent interpretation. Replacing the times with an unrelated convenient value creates misleading evidence, while ignoring the issue may conceal a factor relevant to holding time or result suitability.

lessons.title: Read the report
points: The result is below that reporting threshold, not a measured zero.
Nitrate and nitrate-nitrogen are different expression bases.
It identifies a registered laboratory, not every method's scope at every date.
They can restrict the interpretation or validity of a result.
Match determinand, units, basis, location and applicable requirement.
lessons.intro: Reading a laboratory report means reading more than the result column. Reporting thresholds, method notes, sample condition and analytical scope can all affect interpretation. A result below a reporting threshold is not a measured zero. A laboratory appearing on a register also does not settle every question about a particular test. Match the report to the question being asked, retaining its original units and qualifications.
lessons.example: A spreadsheet converts every result reported as below the laboratory threshold into zero. Before the data are used in a review, you restore the original reporting notation and retain the threshold. This makes the evidence honest about what was and was not measured, allowing later readers to distinguish limited detection from a confirmed absence.

activity.prompt: Which interpretation is supported by a below-threshold report?
options: The determinand is confirmed absent from the entire supply.
The result is below that reporting threshold under the stated method.
The laboratory measured exactly zero.
activity.feedback: The report establishes a result below its stated threshold, not an exact zero or an absence throughout the supply. Preserve the notation and method context in summaries and exports. That allows other reviewers to apply an appropriate interpretation without having to reconstruct information lost during data handling.

lessons.title: Decide and respond
points: Follow the response plan and applicable notification guidance promptly.
Contamination introduced through field handling or materials.
It helps assess variability in sampling and analysis.
Document the missed sample and required corrective action.
It preserves evidence, qualifiers and traceability for review.
lessons.intro: Results become useful when they lead to a proportionate, traceable response. An unexpected finding, missed sample or quality-control concern needs the relevant plan and supporting context. Field blanks and duplicates can answer different questions about the evidence; they are not interchangeable labels. Keep the original report, recorded limitations and follow-up together so another reviewer can understand both the finding and the decision taken in response.
lessons.example: A routine sample was missed because the agreed site could not be accessed. The team records the missed collection, checks the applicable monitoring and response arrangements, and assigns follow-up. They do not fill the gap with a result from a different visit. The review remains transparent about the evidence available for the intended monitoring period.

activity.prompt: Which record best supports a missed-sample review?
options: A copied previous result to keep the schedule complete.
No entry, because an unsuccessful visit produced no sample.
The missed collection, reason, relevant follow-up and responsible person.
activity.feedback: A missed sample is an event to document and manage, not a blank to hide. Recording the reason and follow-up makes accountability and evidence gaps visible. A previous result describes another sample and cannot honestly be used as though it came from the missed collection or monitoring occasion.

courses.title: Small supplies and safety planning
courses.description: Build a practical source-to-tap risk picture for community, rural and school settings.

lessons.title: Know your supply
points: Map the source, treatment, storage, distribution and consumers.
Occupancy and demand may change during the year.
Children, staff, holiday operation and supply-specific hazards.
Faecal contamination risk.
Accountability and response duties must be clear.
lessons.intro: A small supply can still have a complicated journey from source to consumer. Mapping that journey helps people see where treatment, storage, connections and responsibilities begin and end. Seasonal occupancy or a change in users can alter how the supply operates. Start with the actual arrangement and the people who depend on it, rather than assuming that a small number of connections means a simple or low-risk system.
lessons.example: A community facility normally serves a handful of staff but hosts a busy holiday programme. The supply map identifies the source, tank, treatment and drinking outlets, while the operating notes identify who will cover the extra opening days. The team uses the changed occupancy as a prompt to review demand, responsibilities and supply-specific hazards before the programme starts.

activity.prompt: Which change most clearly deserves attention in this supply review?
options: The facility has repainted its entrance sign.
The holiday programme changes demand and the people using the supply.
The supply has few connections, so no operating change matters.
activity.feedback: Changed occupancy can affect demand, operating arrangements and the people exposed to a problem. A supply map and clear responsibilities help the team review those effects. Small size does not remove the need to understand the actual supply, its hazards and its arrangements for normal and abnormal operation.

lessons.title: Source protection
points: Defects can provide contamination pathways into groundwater.
Debris, animals and materials can affect collected water.
Divert an initial portion of runoff with accumulated contamination.
Runoff can carry pathogens and other contaminants.
Assess contamination and follow the supply response plan.
lessons.intro: Source protection looks for practical routes by which contaminants could enter water. A bore defect, animal access to a roof catchment or polluted runoff near an intake each describes a different pathway. The useful inspection question is how the surroundings connect to the collected water. Maintenance and protective features have purposes, so understanding those purposes makes an inspection more valuable than simply ticking that equipment is present.
lessons.example: Following a storm, a caretaker notices damage near the borehead and water pooling around it. They record the condition and follow the supply response plan rather than assuming groundwater is protected because it comes from below ground. The observation connects a physical defect with a possible contamination pathway that needs supply-specific assessment and follow-up.

activity.prompt: What is the most useful way to describe the borehead finding?
options: A possible entry pathway requiring assessment under the supply plan.
An appearance issue unrelated to water because the source is underground.
Proof that the entire aquifer is contaminated.
activity.feedback: The observation identifies a plausible pathway, not a complete conclusion about the aquifer or consumer water. Recording the defect and surrounding conditions supports an appropriate assessment. Follow the supply plan and obtain the relevant evidence instead of dismissing the finding or extending it beyond what was observed.

lessons.title: Storage and treatment
points: They help prevent animals, debris and other contamination entering.
Keeping barriers operating as intended with accountable tasks.
Operators need clear procedures during normal and abnormal operation.
Check compatibility, commissioning and required performance evidence.
Check current eligibility and all conditions for the actual supply.
lessons.intro: Storage and treatment controls need people, procedures and evidence to keep working. A tank lid or screened opening helps prevent contamination entering; a treatment device has operating and maintenance requirements. New equipment should fit the supply and have appropriate commissioning information. Selecting a regulatory pathway also requires checking current conditions and eligibility, rather than assuming that a product description establishes everything the supply needs to demonstrate.
lessons.example: A facility replaces a treatment unit with a newer model and assumes the upgrade is complete once it powers on. During review, the operator asks for the commissioning information, compatibility checks and revised operating tasks. The team treats installation as a change requiring evidence and ownership, instead of regarding a new purchase as automatic proof of suitable performance.

activity.prompt: Which information most directly strengthens the replacement-unit review?
options: The colour of the new unit matches the tank.
The supplier describes the product as modern.
Commissioning, suitability and operating information for the actual installation.
activity.feedback: A product being new or modern does not establish suitable performance in the installed supply. Commissioning and operating information connect the equipment to its intended conditions and tasks. Review the applicable supply arrangements and clarify who will carry out and record the maintenance and monitoring that support ongoing performance.

lessons.title: Plan and respond
points: Hazards, controls, monitoring, responses and improvement actions.
A situation that introduces or increases a hazard.
Consider likelihood, consequences and control effectiveness.
Responsible staff, regulator contacts and relevant support services.
A clear trigger, action, owner and follow-up requirement.
lessons.intro: A safety plan becomes practical when it connects hazards with controls and clear responses. Risk thinking considers likelihood, consequences and whether the controls are effective. A response entry should tell people what triggers action, who acts and what follow-up is needed. The plan is therefore a working guide for the actual supply, not simply a document listing every hazard the writer can imagine in general.
lessons.example: A plan lists heavy rainfall as a concern but says only “check water” in response. The team rewrites the entry around the relevant supply procedure, responsible role and follow-up evidence. They make the connection between the event and the intended decision clearer, so a relief operator can understand what needs attention without guessing the original author’s meaning.

activity.prompt: Which plan entry is more usable during an event?
options: Rain may be a problem; somebody should check eventually.
A defined trigger linked to the relevant action, owner and follow-up.
A long list of hazards with no assigned actions.
activity.feedback: A usable response connects the trigger with action and responsibility. This supports consistent decisions when the usual author is absent. The details must still reflect the actual supply and applicable arrangements; a generic instruction is weak if it leaves the person responding to invent the important operational steps.

lessons.title: People and records
points: Critical tasks must continue when the usual operator is absent.
People need practical and timely protective instructions.
What was done, when, by whom and any follow-up.
It supports traceability and shows whether controls were carried out.
Some groups may face greater consequences from unsafe water.
lessons.intro: People and records are part of the control system. A task that depends on one person’s memory becomes vulnerable when that person is away. Clear handovers show what was done, what remains due and where supporting information can be found. Communication with consumers also needs practical instructions they can understand. Good records support both immediate continuity and later review of how the supply was actually managed.
lessons.example: The caretaker who usually checks a community tank is away for a week. A relief person receives the current task list, recent observations, contact details and any outstanding issues. When a concern arises, the replacement can find the agreed procedure and responsible contact, rather than searching old messages or assuming the absent caretaker has already dealt with it.

activity.prompt: What makes this handover useful?
options: It connects current tasks, evidence, outstanding issues and support contacts.
It relies on the relief person knowing what the caretaker usually remembers.
It avoids mentioning unfinished work so the handover stays brief.
activity.feedback: The handover makes the supply’s current state and responsibilities visible to another person. That supports continuity of critical tasks and timely escalation. A short handover is helpful only if it still contains the information needed to act; concealing outstanding work or relying on memory leaves avoidable gaps.

lessons.title: Review and improve
points: After significant changes, incidents and at required review points.
Finding physical vulnerabilities and contamination pathways.
The activity may change the source risk profile.
Prioritised actions with owners and timeframes to address identified gaps.
Check the current instrument and seek regulator clarification if needed.
lessons.intro: A supply and its surroundings change over time. Incidents, new activities near a source or altered treatment arrangements can reveal weaknesses in an older plan. Review should turn those findings into prioritised improvements with owners and timeframes. Physical inspection and current official information both contribute. Keeping a previous plan unchanged simply because it once appeared adequate misses the opportunity to learn from what the supply is showing now.
lessons.example: A neighbouring property begins a new activity near the source catchment. During review, the operator records the change and considers whether the existing source-risk information remains adequate. An improvement action is assigned to obtain missing information and review relevant controls. The old plan remains a starting point, rather than being treated as proof that new conditions are already addressed.

activity.prompt: Which response best demonstrates active review?
options: Keep the old assessment because it was signed previously.
Assume every neighbouring activity creates the same risk.
Assess the changed context and assign evidence-based follow-up with an owner.
activity.feedback: A review responds to the specific change and identifies what needs to be checked. Assigning an owner and follow-up makes the improvement actionable. A previous signature cannot establish that new conditions are adequately controlled, while assuming an identical risk for every activity skips the context needed for a useful assessment.

courses.title: Wastewater fundamentals
courses.description: Understand collection, treatment, receiving environments and safe operational boundaries.

lessons.title: Collection systems
points: Collect and convey wastewater to appropriate treatment or management.
Groundwater entering through defects or joints.
Rainwater entering through direct connections or openings.
Extra inflow and infiltration can exceed capacity.
Blockages and operational problems.
lessons.intro: Wastewater collection connects households, businesses and other users with treatment or appropriate management. The network can also receive unwanted water through defects or direct rainwater connections. These additional flows matter because they affect capacity and operating conditions. Distinguishing infiltration, inflow and normal wastewater helps you frame an investigation around pathways, rather than treating every increase at the treatment plant as the same type of problem.
lessons.example: A treatment plant receives a sharp increase in flow during rain, even though the connected population has not changed. The network team reviews possible rainwater entry and groundwater infiltration alongside other evidence. They avoid assuming that all extra flow represents more normal wastewater, because different entry pathways call for different investigations and management decisions.

activity.prompt: Which question best starts the wet-weather investigation?
options: Has the same number of people necessarily produced much more sewage?
Where could rainwater or groundwater be entering the collection system?
Can flow information be ignored when the population is unchanged?
activity.feedback: The connection between wet weather and extra flow makes unwanted entry pathways worth investigating. It does not identify the exact defect or connection without further evidence. Separating infiltration and inflow from normal wastewater helps the team understand loading and capacity, while keeping the investigation tied to observations.

lessons.title: Preliminary and primary treatment
points: Large debris and materials that could damage downstream equipment.
Dense abrasive material can wear equipment and accumulate.
Settleable solids separate from the liquid.
Solids settled during primary treatment.
Flow informs loading, capacity and process interpretation.
lessons.intro: Preliminary and primary treatment remove different kinds of material before later processes. Screens intercept larger debris, grit removal addresses dense abrasive particles, and primary settling separates solids that settle under the designed conditions. Following these distinctions helps explain why equipment is placed in sequence. Flow information also matters, because it gives context to the amount of material arriving and the conditions in which separation occurs.
lessons.example: After frequent wear on downstream equipment, a team reviews the material arriving at the plant. They consider whether dense abrasive material is being managed as intended, alongside operating observations and maintenance records. Calling every removed material “screenings” would hide useful distinctions between large debris, grit and the solids separated during primary treatment in the process.

activity.prompt: Which description matches grit removal most closely?
options: Managing dense abrasive material before it causes downstream problems.
Providing oxygen to biological treatment.
Guaranteeing final water is suitable for every possible reuse.
activity.feedback: Grit removal addresses dense abrasive material that can accumulate or wear equipment. That is a different purpose from aeration or final treatment. Correctly naming the function helps connect an operational problem with the relevant evidence, while avoiding the assumption that one preliminary process establishes the performance of the whole plant.

lessons.title: Biological treatment
points: Microorganisms transform biodegradable pollutants under managed conditions.
Provide oxygen and mixing for the biological process.
Biodegradable organic loading under the test conditions.
Biological oxidation of ammonia toward nitrite and nitrate.
Biological reduction of nitrate under suitable anoxic conditions.
lessons.intro: Biological treatment relies on microorganisms operating under managed conditions. Oxygen, mixing and other process conditions support particular transformations of pollutants. Organic loading and nitrogen processes describe different aspects of the work taking place. Understanding those distinctions helps you ask useful operational questions without assuming that every biological tank has the same role or that one test result describes all of the processes occurring within it.
lessons.example: A learner sees a high organic loading indicator and a separate discussion about nitrogen removal in the same shift report. They trace which observations relate to biodegradable organic material, ammonia oxidation and nitrate reduction. The exercise prevents the learner from combining different biological processes into one vague idea that “the microbes remove everything” at the plant.

activity.prompt: Which statement best separates these biological processes?
options: All biological transformations need identical conditions.
Organic loading results automatically describe every nitrogen transformation.
Different transformations have different roles and suitable operating conditions.
activity.feedback: Biological treatment includes processes with different functions and conditions. Keeping those roles separate helps interpret the evidence and ask focused questions. Introductory understanding supports discussion with the operating team, but it does not establish a specific plant’s settings or replace its procedures and competent process assessment.

lessons.title: Solids and final treatment
points: Control biomass inventory and process conditions.
Separated solids still require appropriate treatment and management.
Reduce viable pathogens before the intended discharge or use.
They can reduce transmission or shield microorganisms.
The intended use, treatment performance and applicable requirements.
lessons.intro: Separating solids does not make their management disappear. Solids streams need appropriate handling, while the final liquid may need further treatment suited to its intended discharge or use. Remaining particles can also affect disinfection performance. Think of the plant as connected liquid and solids pathways: success in one separation stage creates another stream to manage, rather than ending responsibility for the material that has been removed.
lessons.example: A process diagram shows clarified liquid leaving one stage but stops at the arrow labelled “sludge”. The learner adds the next management questions for that solids stream and identifies the final liquid’s intended destination. This makes the diagram more honest about where material goes and what evidence is needed beyond the separation step.

activity.prompt: What is missing when a diagram ends at the sludge arrow?
options: Recognition that separated solids still need appropriate treatment and management.
Proof that solids no longer contain anything requiring attention.
An assumption that only the final liquid matters environmentally.
activity.feedback: Separated solids remain a management responsibility. Following their pathway helps identify the next treatment and handling questions instead of treating removal as disappearance. The final liquid has its own intended use or discharge context, so the evidence for both streams needs to match the relevant process and requirements.

lessons.title: Environment and monitoring
points: The water, land or other environment receiving a discharge.
Help distinguish background conditions from discharge effects.
The current consent or other applicable authorisation and its conditions.
Load also depends on flow.
Excessive plant or algal growth under suitable receiving conditions.
lessons.intro: Environmental interpretation needs more than a concentration printed on a report. Flow contributes to pollutant load, and receiving-environment conditions affect how effects are understood. Upstream and downstream observations may help separate background conditions from potential discharge influences. The applicable consent or other authorisation provides essential context. Read these pieces together before concluding that a single favourable number establishes acceptable environmental performance across all conditions and occasions.
lessons.example: Two days show the same effluent concentration, but the discharge flow is much higher on the second day. A reviewer recognises that equal concentrations do not necessarily mean equal loads. They also review the receiving conditions and applicable authorisation, keeping the calculation question separate from any conclusion about whether the discharge meets its requirements.

activity.prompt: What can be concluded from equal concentrations on the two days?
options: The pollutant loads must be identical.
Load comparison also needs the discharge flow information.
The receiving environment and authorisation are irrelevant.
activity.feedback: Concentration alone cannot establish equal loads when flow changes. Bringing flow into the review answers a different question from concentration comparison. Environmental assessment also needs the receiving context and applicable authorisation, so avoid converting a useful calculation into an unsupported overall statement about compliance or environmental effects.

lessons.title: Safe operations
points: Hazardous atmospheres, engulfment and other dangers may be present.
Keep clear and follow trained emergency and site procedures.
Prevent unintended energisation or movement.
Follow response, public protection and applicable reporting procedures.
Knowledge of introductory concepts, not practical operator competence.
lessons.intro: Wastewater facilities can present serious hazards, including hazardous atmospheres and unexpected movement of equipment. Introductory process knowledge does not authorise entry, rescue or maintenance activities. Safe work relies on the relevant site procedures, training and roles. Recognising when to keep clear and involve appropriately trained people is an important learning outcome, especially when an urgent event makes improvised action feel tempting to someone unfamiliar with the site.
lessons.example: During a site visit, a learner sees a colleague become unresponsive near a confined-space opening. The learner keeps clear and raises the alarm through the site emergency arrangements instead of attempting an unplanned entry. The example shows why knowing treatment terminology cannot substitute for the training, equipment and coordinated procedures needed in a hazardous situation.

activity.prompt: Which action reflects the boundary of introductory learning?
options: Enter immediately because knowing the process makes entry safe.
Switch equipment repeatedly until the colleague responds.
Keep clear and activate the trained emergency response arrangements.
activity.feedback: Introductory learning does not make hazardous entry or improvised rescue safe. Keeping clear and activating the site response avoids creating another casualty. Follow the established emergency arrangements and trained roles; a completion record from this learning resource is not practical competence or authorisation to perform hazardous tasks.

courses.title: Stormwater and resilient places
courses.description: Connect runoff, flooding, water quality and blue-green approaches.

lessons.title: Runoff and catchments
points: Rainwater that flows across surfaces rather than infiltrating or evaporating.
They generally reduce infiltration and can increase runoff.
The area draining toward a specified outlet.
Wet soils can have less remaining infiltration capacity.
Runoff volume, peak flow and pollutant pathways.
lessons.intro: Stormwater connects rainfall with the shape and condition of a catchment. Water may infiltrate, evaporate or move across surfaces toward an outlet. Roofs and paved areas influence that balance, while soil wetness affects how much more water can enter the ground. Looking at the catchment as a connected area helps explain why changes at one property may affect runoff volume, timing or pathways somewhere else downstream.
lessons.example: A community centre replaces a planted area with a paved courtyard. A learner sketches where rain previously entered the ground and where runoff may now travel. They include the receiving drain and downstream area instead of stopping at the property boundary. The sketch becomes a question for site-specific assessment, rather than a claim that the change has no wider effect.

activity.prompt: Why include the downstream area in the sketch?
options: Runoff connections can carry the effect beyond the changed surface.
A property boundary stops water movement automatically.
Only the colour of the new paving affects runoff.
activity.feedback: Catchments connect surfaces and outlets, so a local change can affect water movement beyond the work area. Mapping that connection supports useful questions about runoff. It does not quantify the effect on its own; site conditions and appropriate assessment are needed before making design or risk conclusions.

lessons.title: Water quality
points: Flow can pick up sediment, litter, metals and other contaminants.
It can cloud water and harm aquatic habitats.
Wastewater may be entering a stormwater system.
Stormwater may lead to waterways without full treatment.
Pollutants accumulated on surfaces before rainfall.
lessons.intro: Rainwater can pick up material as it moves across streets, yards and disturbed ground. Sediment, litter and other contaminants may therefore reach waterways through drainage systems. A stormwater drain is not necessarily a route to full wastewater treatment. Understanding the flow path gives everyday pollution prevention a clear purpose: keeping unwanted material out before rainfall carries it somewhere that is harder to protect or clean up.
lessons.example: A workshop employee prepares to rinse paint residue into an outdoor drain because it looks like the nearest disposal point. A colleague checks the drainage context and points out the potential connection to receiving waters. The team follows the appropriate waste-handling arrangements instead of assuming that anything poured into a drain will receive treatment before discharge.

activity.prompt: Which assumption should be challenged?
options: Outdoor drainage may connect to a waterway.
Every drain leads to full wastewater treatment.
Material left on a surface can be carried by rain.
activity.feedback: The destination and treatment of drainage cannot be assumed from the presence of a drain opening. Stormwater can reach waterways without full treatment. Keeping paint, washwater and other unwanted material out supports pollution prevention, while the appropriate disposal arrangements should be checked for the actual material and site.

lessons.title: Blue-green systems
points: Manage runoff using designed vegetation, soil and drainage processes.
Infiltration or storage where site conditions and design allow.
Runoff attenuation, water quality treatment and habitat when appropriately designed.
Temporarily store runoff and release it at a controlled rate.
Several measures can manage different runoff issues along the flow path.
lessons.intro: Blue-green systems use designed combinations of vegetation, soils, storage and drainage to manage runoff. Their functions can include slowing flow, treating water or supporting habitat, depending on design and conditions. Different measures can work together along a flow path. Recognising the intended function of each part helps learners see these systems as maintained infrastructure, rather than assuming that any planted patch will manage every stormwater issue automatically.
lessons.example: A neighbourhood project proposes a rain garden near a busy paved area. The learner asks what runoff it will receive, what role it is designed to perform and how it will be maintained. These questions distinguish a functioning stormwater measure from decorative planting and connect the visible landscape with the less visible soil and drainage components beneath it.

activity.prompt: Which question best examines the rain garden’s stormwater function?
options: Will its flowers match the nearest building?
Can any planted area manage unlimited runoff?
What runoff, treatment role and maintenance arrangements are intended?
activity.feedback: A blue-green measure needs an understood function and suitable conditions. Asking about the incoming runoff, intended role and upkeep connects the landscape to its infrastructure purpose. Appearance alone does not establish capacity or performance, and introductory learning does not replace the assessment and design needed for the particular site.

lessons.title: Flood resilience
points: A route water can take across the ground when drainage capacity is exceeded.
Obstructions can redirect floodwater and increase risk.
It can conceal strong currents, contaminants and physical hazards.
Changing rainfall and sea-level conditions can alter flood risk.
Moving water faster can transfer risk to others.
lessons.intro: Flood resilience includes the routes water may take when drainage capacity is exceeded. Overland flow paths can cross areas that appear dry in normal weather, and obstructions may redirect water toward other people or property. Floodwater itself can conceal serious hazards. Understanding these pathways encourages decisions that consider the wider area, rather than treating rapid removal from one location as proof that risk has been reduced overall.
lessons.example: A resident proposes a barrier across a low area to keep stormwater away from a garage. The map and ground shape suggest that this area also carries overland flow. A learner recognises the need for site-specific advice about redirected water, instead of assuming that a barrier benefiting one doorway will improve flood outcomes for the surrounding properties.

activity.prompt: What is the key concern with the proposed barrier?
options: It may redirect floodwater and change risk elsewhere.
Any barrier necessarily reduces the total flood risk.
Dry-weather appearance proves the low area never carries water.
activity.feedback: An obstruction can change where water travels when drainage is exceeded. That makes the wider flow path relevant to the proposal. A local benefit is not proof of an overall reduction in risk, so seek appropriate site-specific assessment and keep people away from floodwater and its concealed hazards.

lessons.title: Design and evidence
points: An assumed rainfall event used for a defined design assessment.
Mapping may be approximate, outdated or unsuitable for detailed design.
Soils, groundwater, contamination, structures and applicable design requirements.
Local conditions and regulatory requirements vary.
Devices need safe inspection, cleaning and servicing.
lessons.intro: Stormwater evidence has a scale and purpose. A broad map can identify matters to investigate, while a detailed design needs suitable local information and assumptions. Soil, groundwater, contamination and nearby structures can affect whether a proposed approach is appropriate. Treat a design rainfall event as an assessment assumption, not a prediction that every future storm will behave exactly the same way at the selected site.
lessons.example: An online map suggests that part of a property may be exposed to flooding. The owner asks whether the coloured boundary is precise enough to set a building level. A learner explains that the map is a starting point for investigation and that detailed decisions need appropriate local evidence, current requirements and qualified assessment for the proposed work.

activity.prompt: How should the broad online map be used?
options: As a guaranteed property-level design without further checking.
As screening information whose suitability and limitations need review.
As proof that areas outside the colour can never flood.
activity.feedback: A map’s purpose and resolution limit what it can establish. Screening information can identify a concern without supplying all the evidence for detailed design. Review local conditions, assumptions and applicable requirements with appropriately qualified input rather than treating a coloured boundary as an exact guarantee about future water levels.

lessons.title: Care and response
points: Condition, defects, date, location and follow-up actions.
Blockage and accumulated material can reduce performance.
Inspect, repair and document actions promptly under the site plan.
Keep litter, paint, washwater and spills out of stormwater drains.
Introductory learning alongside qualified site-specific assessment.
lessons.intro: Stormwater measures need care after installation. Blockage, accumulated material and damage can reduce the performance intended by the design. Inspection records help connect a finding with its location, date and follow-up, while safe access and servicing matter for the people doing the work. Everyday prevention also contributes: less litter and fewer pollutants entering the system means fewer avoidable problems for devices and receiving waters downstream.
lessons.example: A school rain garden repeatedly ponds in an unexpected location after rain. The caretaker photographs the condition from a safe position, records the date and location, and raises follow-up under the maintenance arrangements. The team reviews blockage or damage rather than assuming that unusual ponding must be a normal feature simply because the garden was recently built.

activity.prompt: Which record is most useful for follow-up?
options: A message saying only that the garden looks strange.
A statement that new infrastructure cannot need maintenance.
A dated location record, observed condition and assigned follow-up.
activity.feedback: A specific record allows the right people to find the issue and evaluate whether action is needed. Recent construction does not remove maintenance needs. Keep observation separate from diagnosis, and use the site’s safe inspection and servicing arrangements when investigating blockage, damage or other possible causes of reduced performance.

courses.title: Backflow awareness
courses.description: Spot cross-connections and understand prevention without implying tester certification.

lessons.title: Mechanisms
points: Unintended reversal of water flow into a supply system.
Reverse flow caused by a reduction in supply pressure.
A downstream pressure higher than the upstream supply pressure.
An actual or potential pathway between potable water and another source.
Yes; temporary hoses and equipment can create contamination pathways.
lessons.intro: Backflow describes water moving in the unintended direction through a connection. A drop in supply pressure can create backsiphonage, while a higher downstream pressure can create backpressure. The connection makes the reversal important because water or contaminants may return toward the drinking water supply. Separating the mechanism from the hazard helps you explain both how reverse flow could occur and why the connected activity needs appropriate protection.
lessons.example: A temporary hose remains connected to a vessel while supply pressure falls during nearby work. The learner sketches the connection and identifies the pressure change as a possible backsiphonage condition. They do not need to invent a measured reverse flow to recognise the pathway; the scenario is a prompt for appropriate assessment and protection of the actual connection.

activity.prompt: Which mechanism fits the drop in supply pressure?
options: Backpressure from a permanently higher supply pressure.
Backsiphonage under the reduced supply-pressure condition.
No mechanism, because the hose is temporary.
activity.feedback: Reduced supply pressure can create conditions for backsiphonage where a relevant connection exists. The temporary nature of a hose does not remove the pathway. Recognising a plausible mechanism supports appropriate assessment, but it is not proof that reverse flow occurred during this particular event without further evidence.

lessons.title: Common hazards
points: It creates a potential pathway back into the supply.
Fertilisers, chemicals or soil contamination may be connected to the system.
Processes can introduce contaminants with different hazard levels.
A contamination hazard requiring appropriate assessment.
The contamination hazard may change.
lessons.intro: Backflow hazards often arise from ordinary activities rather than unusual equipment. Hoses, irrigation arrangements and process connections can place drinking water in contact with other materials. What is connected matters, and that activity can change over time. An old assessment may therefore need review when the use changes. Focus on the possible contamination pathway and connected hazard, rather than assuming that familiar equipment is harmless because it has always been there.
lessons.example: A garden hose previously used to fill a clean container is now used around fertiliser-mixing equipment. The learner identifies the changed activity as relevant to the connection assessment. The hose itself may look unchanged, but the substances and potential contamination pathway around its use differ from the arrangement considered earlier by the people responsible for the site.

activity.prompt: Why review the connection after this change?
options: The connected hazard may have changed even though the hose looks the same.
A familiar hose can never create a contamination pathway.
Only a change to the pipe diameter can matter.
activity.feedback: A connection assessment depends on the hazard and use, not only the appearance of the hardware. A changed activity can introduce different contaminants or pathways. Bring that change to the responsible people for appropriate review rather than assuming that the earlier arrangement remains suitable for every later use.

lessons.title: Protection selection
points: Hazard, mechanism, applicable requirements and site conditions.
Physical separation between a water outlet and a receiving vessel.
Different devices provide different protection under different conditions.
Appropriately competent or authorised people following applicable requirements.
The device must suit the required application and requirements.
lessons.intro: Protection selection connects a hazard and backflow mechanism with suitable measures and applicable requirements. Different devices do not provide identical protection in every situation, and physical separation has a different role from a mechanical assembly. Introductory awareness helps you recognise the selection questions, but the actual choice requires appropriately competent or authorised input. A product being available or labelled as a check valve does not establish suitability for every application.
lessons.example: A purchasing team finds a low-cost device described as preventing reverse flow. Before ordering it for a process connection, a learner asks whether the hazard, mechanism and installation conditions have been assessed. The team refers the selection to the appropriate person instead of treating a general product description as a complete assessment for the site’s actual requirements.

activity.prompt: What should guide the device selection?
options: The lowest price among devices with similar names.
The assumption that every non-return device suits every hazard.
Assessed hazard, mechanism, site conditions and applicable requirements.
activity.feedback: Protection needs to match the assessed application. Similar names and broad product descriptions do not establish equivalent protection. Appropriate selection considers the hazard, possible mechanism and installation context, with competent or authorised input as required. Introductory learning supports those questions but does not grant authority to select or install protection independently.

lessons.title: Installation and access
points: Inspection, testing, maintenance and safe operation need access.
Some devices can discharge water and need safe drainage.
An unprotected bypass can defeat the intended barrier.
Flooding, freezing or damage can compromise function.
Asset location, type and identification support ongoing management.
lessons.intro: A suitable protective device still needs a suitable installation. Access supports inspection and testing, environmental exposure can affect condition, and some assemblies need safe drainage arrangements. A bypass can also undermine the intended barrier if it creates an unprotected route. Looking at the whole installed arrangement is therefore essential; reading a device label alone will miss practical features that affect how protection is maintained over time.
lessons.example: A new cabinet neatly encloses an existing assembly, but leaves little space for access and obscures its identification. A learner flags the change for review before assuming that a tidier enclosure is automatically an improvement. The discussion considers safe inspection, servicing and identification, connecting the visible building work with the ongoing management of the protection.

activity.prompt: Which feature needs review after the cabinet is installed?
options: Whether access and identification still support required inspection and servicing.
Whether the cabinet makes the device disappear from routine records.
Whether a neat appearance proves all performance requirements are met.
activity.feedback: Access and identification support ongoing inspection, testing and maintenance. An enclosure can change those practical conditions even without replacing the assembly. A neat appearance is useful only alongside an arrangement that allows the protection to be managed appropriately; review the actual installation rather than relying on the device label alone.

lessons.title: Inspection and testing
points: Visible condition, not every aspect of internal performance.
Testing needs reliable and consistent evidence.
Required corrective action, documentation and follow-up testing.
They support traceability and ongoing obligations.
No; practical competence and any required authorisation are separate.
lessons.intro: Inspection and testing provide different kinds of evidence. An assembly may appear intact while its internal performance remains unconfirmed. Reliable test equipment, competent procedures and traceable records help establish the condition relevant to ongoing obligations. A failed result needs corrective action and follow-up under the applicable arrangements. Completing an introductory quiz is useful awareness, but it does not replace practical competence or any authorisation needed to perform testing.
lessons.example: A site record says “looks fine” beside an assembly for which performance evidence is requested. The learner asks whether this was a visual inspection or an appropriate test and who completed it. The distinction helps the manager locate the relevant evidence instead of treating a brief appearance note as proof that every internal function has been demonstrated.

activity.prompt: What does the visual note establish on its own?
options: Every internal function passed the required performance test.
Only the observed external condition within the inspection’s scope.
The learner is now authorised to carry out formal testing.
activity.feedback: A visual inspection has a limited scope. It cannot automatically substitute for the performance evidence required from appropriate testing. Clarify what was done, by whom and with what records, and use competent or authorised personnel where required. A learning completion record does not establish practical testing competence.

lessons.title: Incident response
points: Follow the response plan, protect consumers and seek appropriate technical and regulator advice.
It may create conditions for ingress or backsiphonage.
Investigate and assess the hazard rather than assume protection.
Different parties may control different parts of protection.
Identify hazards, provide appropriate protection and maintain evidence.
lessons.intro: A suspected backflow incident calls for coordinated protection and investigation. Pressure history, connections, possible contaminants and affected areas can all matter. Different parties may control different parts of the installation, so clear responsibilities support an effective response. Follow the relevant response plan and obtain appropriate technical and regulator advice rather than assuming a device’s presence proves there could be no issue or that an unplanned adjustment will resolve it.
lessons.example: After a pressure interruption, a consumer reports an unusual change near a commercial connection. The site team preserves the report and relevant operating information, checks responsibilities and follows the response arrangements. They seek appropriate support for the connection review instead of closing the concern solely because a protective device appears on an old asset list.

activity.prompt: Which response best preserves useful evidence?
options: Dismiss the report because a device appears in the asset list.
Assume the report proves exactly which contaminant entered.
Record the event and follow the plan while the connection and protection are assessed.
activity.feedback: An asset entry is useful background but does not settle an incident investigation. Recording the reported change and following the response arrangements preserves a basis for assessment. Avoid both dismissal and unsupported diagnosis; the relevant people need the connection, pressure and protection evidence to determine the appropriate next steps.

courses.title: Public health and water incidents
courses.description: Recognise exposure pathways, evidence limitations and clear protective communication.

lessons.title: Hazards and exposure
points: Exposure and the likelihood and consequences of harm.
Through drinking, food preparation and other relevant uses.
Some can cause illness at low exposure levels.
Their sources, health effects and effective controls differ.
No; harmful contaminants may not change taste.
lessons.intro: Water hazards become public health concerns through exposure and the possibility of harm. Drinking, preparing food and other relevant uses can create different exposure situations. Microbial and chemical hazards also differ in their sources and effective controls. Sensory qualities are not a complete safety test: water may look or taste acceptable while still presenting a hazard. Begin by identifying the hazard and exposure context before discussing a protective response.
lessons.example: A family asks whether water is safe because it has no unusual taste. A learner explains that taste alone cannot answer the question and directs them to the current supplier or authority information. The discussion separates sensory observations from evidence about the particular hazard and the uses covered by any current advice for the affected area.

activity.prompt: Which statement best answers the taste question?
options: Acceptable taste rules out every health hazard.
Taste is one observation and cannot establish safety on its own.
Any unusual taste identifies a particular pathogen.
activity.feedback: Taste cannot confirm the absence of harmful contaminants or identify every hazard. The appropriate interpretation needs relevant evidence and current advice for the affected supply. Keep sensory observations in context and help people find the official information that addresses their location, water uses and any protective instructions.

lessons.title: Risk and vulnerability
points: They may be more vulnerable to particular water hazards.
Hazard is potential harm; risk considers the likelihood and consequences.
Some health effects depend on exposure over time.
Manage risks across the full supply chain.
Waiting for confirmed illness may leave people exposed.
lessons.intro: Risk thinking brings likelihood, consequences and the effectiveness of controls together. Different people can experience different consequences from the same water problem, and some effects depend on exposure over time. A source-to-consumer view helps locate controls before exposure occurs. Waiting for confirmed illness is therefore a weak substitute for responding to relevant evidence of a hazard or a failure in the arrangements intended to protect consumers.
lessons.example: A community service is reviewing how a supply incident might affect its users, including people with additional health needs. The team maps where exposure could occur and how practical advice would reach those users. They do not assume that a general message on a website reaches everyone or that absence of reported illness means no protective planning is needed.

activity.prompt: What adds the most value to this review?
options: Considering exposure, potentially greater consequences and accessible communication.
Assuming every consumer has identical needs and access.
Waiting for illness reports before examining the exposure pathways.
activity.feedback: Exposure and consequences help explain why different users may need particular attention in planning and communication. An absence of reported illness does not establish an absence of risk. Use relevant evidence and the applicable response arrangements to protect people, while making the advice accessible to those who need it.

lessons.title: Interpreting evidence
points: Possible faecal contamination requiring the appropriate response.
The target was not detected under the test conditions.
They establish which conditions the result represents.
Health interpretation also requires exposure, context and relevant guidance.
Unconfirmed or requiring verification, with clear next steps.
lessons.intro: Evidence supports careful conclusions when its limits remain visible. An indicator result may point to a concern requiring response, while a non-detect result describes what the test found under its conditions. Neither should be stretched into claims about every place and time. Site, timing, method and exposure context help determine what the evidence means and what additional information or action is needed for a public health decision.
lessons.example: A recent sample did not detect the target organism, but a later incident affects a different part of the network. A learner identifies the result’s location and time before using it in the incident summary. This preserves a useful observation without implying that one earlier sample proves conditions throughout the affected area remained unchanged during the subsequent event.

activity.prompt: Which summary respects the result’s scope?
options: The entire network was certainly safe throughout the later incident.
The result makes the incident report irrelevant.
The target was not detected in that sample under the test conditions.
activity.feedback: The sample result is tied to its site, time and method. It remains useful evidence, but it does not establish conditions throughout a different area or later event. Preserve that context and identify the additional evidence needed rather than converting a limited non-detect finding into an unrestricted safety claim.

lessons.title: Protective notices
points: Give specific protective instructions for the identified microbial concern.
No; boiling does not remove nitrate and can concentrate it as water evaporates.
The official notice and its stated uses, restrictions and alternatives.
The issuing authority's specific restrictions and advice.
The responsible authority or supplier following the applicable evidence and process.
lessons.intro: Protective water notices are specific instructions for a defined concern, area and set of uses. A boil-water notice addresses certain microbial concerns, but boiling is not a general solution to every contaminant. Other notices may impose different restrictions and alternatives. Read the current official wording carefully and preserve those distinctions when communicating with others, rather than replacing different notice types with a familiar instruction that may not address the identified hazard.
lessons.example: Someone forwards an old boil-water message into a discussion about a current chemical concern. The learner redirects the group to the current official notice and its stated uses and alternatives. They explain that boiling does not remove nitrate and can concentrate it as water evaporates, so advice for a different hazard should not be substituted for the current instructions.

activity.prompt: Which message should guide affected consumers?
options: The current official notice for the specific concern, area and uses.
Whichever past notice is easiest to find online.
A general instruction to boil water for every possible contaminant.
activity.feedback: Protective advice must match the identified concern. An old message or generic boiling instruction may fail to address a chemical hazard. Use the current notice and its stated restrictions and alternatives, retaining the responsible authority’s wording and context rather than improvising or combining incompatible instructions from separate incidents.

lessons.title: Incident management
points: Time, evidence, affected area, actions and responsible people.
Updates need clear ownership and consistent verified messages.
Who is affected, what to do, alternatives and where to find updates.
It supports coordination, accountability and later review.
Reassess the response and communicate verified changes.
lessons.intro: Incident management depends on a shared account of what is known and who is doing what. Time, location, evidence, actions and responsibilities help people coordinate an evolving response. Public messages also need clear ownership so verified updates reach the affected group consistently. Separate confirmed information from matters still being checked, and make the next source of updates clear instead of presenting early assumptions as final conclusions to the public.
lessons.example: Two teams receive different versions of an affected-area description during an incident. The coordinator checks the evidence, identifies the current authorised update and records the correction and its timing. People responsible for public communication use the same verified information, reducing confusion about who is affected and where consumers should look for the next update.

activity.prompt: What most directly improves the inconsistent messages?
options: Let each team publish whichever area description they first received.
Confirm a shared verified update and clear communication ownership.
Remove all times so readers cannot compare changing information.
activity.feedback: A shared verified update and clear ownership support consistent communication while the incident evolves. Keeping times helps readers distinguish current information from older versions. Record the evidence and corrections so the response remains traceable, while avoiding claims about affected areas that the responsible team has not established.

lessons.title: Learning and recovery
points: Evidence, completed controls and the applicable release process.
Identify causes, lessons and improvements.
A message is effective only if affected people can access and understand it.
Handle it lawfully with appropriate privacy and access controls.
It records learning and does not replace trained response roles.
lessons.intro: Recovery is more than the disappearance of an alarming reading. It needs appropriate evidence, completed controls and the relevant process for changing protective advice. Afterwards, a review should identify causes, lessons and improvements without exposing personal information unnecessarily. Communication also deserves review: a technically correct message only helps if affected people can access and understand it. Learning from the response strengthens future readiness as well as closing the immediate event.
lessons.example: After an incident, a community group reports that the online update was hard to understand and unavailable to several users. The review records this alongside the technical actions and evidence. The improvement plan includes clearer communication responsibilities and accessible channels, rather than judging the response successful solely because a notice appeared on the supplier’s website.

activity.prompt: Which lesson should the review retain?
options: Publication alone proves every affected person received usable advice.
Only technical measurements belong in a response review.
Accessibility and understanding matter alongside the technical recovery evidence.
activity.feedback: Public protection depends partly on people being able to act on the advice. Review whether messages were accessible and understandable alongside technical evidence and completed actions. Keep personal information appropriately protected, and assign practical improvements rather than assuming that posting an update was sufficient for every affected group.
