courses.title: Wai, tikanga and respectful practice
courses.description: Build awareness of relationships, local authority and careful use of cultural knowledge.

lessons.title: Relationships with wai
points: Relationships with wai can include whakapapa, identity, wellbeing and spiritual dimensions.
Whakapapa, mātauranga and tikanga.
Genealogical relationships and connections.
Māori knowledge and ways of knowing.
Appropriate customs and practices shaped by context and community.
lessons.intro: Wai can hold relationships extending beyond its physical use as a resource. Whakapapa, identity, wellbeing, mātauranga and spiritual dimensions may all be relevant, with meaning grounded in particular people and places. An introductory resource can help learners recognise that breadth, but it cannot speak for every community. Approach the topic through attentive listening and local relationships rather than reducing tikanga to a universal checklist of customs for water projects.
lessons.example: A project team describes a stream only as a drainage channel in its first briefing. A learner asks what relationships and knowledge may be missing from that description and who should guide a fuller local understanding. The question opens space for appropriate engagement without assuming that the learner can supply the community’s interpretation from a general online summary.

activity.prompt: Which response best reflects introductory awareness?
options: Recognise the limits of the technical description and seek appropriate local guidance.
Replace the description with an invented traditional story.
Assume every stream has identical cultural relationships.
activity.feedback: Recognising a missing perspective is a useful first step, but it is not authority to invent or supply that perspective. Local relationships and appropriate knowledge holders guide understanding. Treat the introductory resource as a prompt for respectful engagement rather than a substitute for community-specific knowledge and tikanga.

lessons.title: Local engagement
points: Appropriate local relationships and authority matter.
Early enough to help shape the work and decisions.
Ask appropriate local people how to proceed.
Practices and authority can be place- and community-specific.
Relevant people, purpose, process, responsibilities and follow-through.
lessons.intro: Respectful engagement begins early enough for the relevant people to help shape the work. It involves clarifying who should participate, what the purpose is and how responsibilities and follow-through will be handled. Authority and practice can be specific to place and community. A familiar contact or a generic process therefore should not be assumed to represent everyone whose relationships or interests are relevant to a proposed water project.
lessons.example: A team plans to contact local representatives only after completing its preferred design. A learner suggests clarifying appropriate relationships and process while the project is still being shaped. This changes engagement from a late presentation into an opportunity to understand priorities and responsibilities before assumptions are locked into decisions that may be difficult to revisit later.

activity.prompt: Which timing best supports meaningful input?
options: Only after every major decision has been finalised.
Early enough for appropriate people to help shape the work.
Whenever the team wants a photograph for its final report.
activity.feedback: Early engagement allows relevant people to influence the work rather than simply hear about a completed decision. Clarify the appropriate participants, purpose and process for the place involved. Timing alone is not enough; respectful follow-through and clear responsibilities are also needed to honour what has been discussed or agreed.

lessons.title: Knowledge and authority
points: The appropriate knowledge holders and people with authority.
Origin and context affect meaning and appropriate use.
No; traditional attribution requires a reliable source and context.
As an original reflection rather than a traditional saying.
A general summary may miss relationships and context.
lessons.intro: Knowledge has origins, context and people with authority to share or interpret it. A phrase found online is not automatically a verified traditional saying or suitable for a project’s public materials. Checking provenance helps avoid invented attribution and loss of meaning. When writing a new reflection, identify it honestly as original writing rather than presenting it as inherited knowledge or community endorsement that the author has not established.
lessons.example: A colleague suggests placing a water-themed sentence on a slide and labelling it a traditional whakataukī, but no reliable source can be found. The learner recommends removing the traditional attribution or using a properly sourced, contextually appropriate alternative. This preserves honesty about the team’s writing without implying an authority or history that the available evidence does not support.

activity.prompt: What is the soundest response to the unverified attribution?
options: Keep it because the wording sounds culturally appropriate.
Attribute it to the nearest local community without asking.
Remove the unsupported traditional claim and identify any original writing honestly.
activity.feedback: A traditional attribution is a claim about provenance, not a stylistic decoration. Without a reliable source and context, it should not be invented. Original reflections can be presented honestly as original writing, while material attributed to knowledge holders needs appropriate verification and consideration of permission and intended use.

lessons.title: Data care
points: Consider permission, sensitivity and who may be affected.
Material can be visible online while its reuse remains restricted or inappropriate.
Authority, provenance, purpose, access and kaitiaki interests.
Authority, confidentiality and permitted use may be unresolved.
Purpose, access, sharing, retention and responsibilities.
lessons.intro: Information about wai can include sensitivities that a simple public-versus-private label misses. Material visible online may still have limits around reuse, interpretation or wider distribution. Data care therefore considers origin, authority, purpose, access and the people who could be affected. Clarifying those matters before sharing supports responsible relationships and avoids treating technical convenience as permission to expose or repurpose information beyond the context in which it was provided.
lessons.example: A project member finds a detailed location map online and wants to add it to an unrestricted public dashboard. The learner pauses to ask about provenance, sensitivity and permission for that new use. Public visibility is treated as one fact about access, rather than as automatic authority to republish all details or remove the map’s original context.

activity.prompt: What needs checking before the dashboard publication?
options: Provenance, authority, sensitivity and permission for the proposed use.
Only whether the file can be downloaded quickly.
Nothing, because any visible material is unrestricted.
activity.feedback: Access does not automatically establish unrestricted reuse. Considering provenance, authority and potential effects helps determine whether the proposed sharing is appropriate. Clarify purpose and permissions with the relevant people, and retain any agreed limits instead of assuming that a technically available file is free of contextual responsibilities.

lessons.title: Respectful communication
points: Accurate wording, attribution, context and appropriate permission.
They support accurate spelling and meaning.
Its source, context and any limits or need for local review.
Listen, clarify authority and context, and review the content appropriately.
Invented attribution, sensitive details and claims to speak for mana whenua.
lessons.intro: Respectful communication depends on accurate wording, context and an honest account of who is speaking. Macrons support correct spelling and meaning, while attribution and permissions help preserve relationships around the material. If feedback identifies a concern, listening and clarifying the issue is more useful than defending an unverified interpretation. A general website summary should make its limitations clear and avoid implying that it represents all mana whenua or every local practice.
lessons.example: A reviewer points out a missing macron and questions whether a paragraph implies endorsement by local mana whenua. Correcting the page becomes a chance to improve accuracy and context rather than merely adjust its visual style.

activity.feedback: Spelling, attribution and implied authority all contribute to meaning. Clarifying who wrote the summary and obtaining appropriate review addresses more than presentation. An introductory label does not justify inaccurate language or an unsupported endorsement claim; use feedback to improve the account and its context with the relevant people.

lessons.title: Applying the learning
points: Introductory awareness, not mana whenua authority or cultural accreditation.
Understand their roles and engage appropriately without treating one generic summary as universal.
Legal duties and cultural relationships have different sources and can change.
Record agreed actions and honour commitments with appropriate review.
Build respectful relationships with the relevant people and learn the local context.
lessons.intro: Applying this learning means building habits of respectful inquiry and follow-through. It does not grant cultural authority or substitute for local relationships. A team can identify relevant people, clarify agreed actions and revisit its assumptions as work develops. Legal duties and cultural relationships also have different sources, so avoid treating one general summary as a complete account of either. Continue learning from the appropriate context rather than collecting a certificate as proof of expertise.
lessons.example: At the end of a project meeting, the team has several agreed follow-up actions but no named owners. A learner suggests confirming responsibilities, recording what may be shared and setting an appropriate review point. This practical step supports the relationship through delivery, rather than treating attendance at the meeting as evidence that every commitment has already been fulfilled.

activity.feedback: Respectful practice continues after a meeting through clear responsibilities and honoured commitments. Confirming actions and permitted use supports that continuity. A quiz result records introductory learning only; it does not confer mana whenua authority, cultural accreditation or the right to speak for people whose knowledge and relationships are involved.

courses.title: Water safety plans
courses.description: Build a practical catchment-to-consumer risk plan, assign controls and turn review findings into action.

sources.title: WHO water safety plan manual, second edition

lessons.title: Describe the supply
lessons.intro: A useful system description follows actual water routes, dependencies and operating modes. Drawings need checking against what staff find on site, including bypasses, seasonal sources and unusual operating arrangements. Show where raw water becomes treated water and where the supply can mix with other sources. Include the operating states used during maintenance and emergencies, not just the most common flow path. Mark who operates each asset and how its condition becomes known to the team.
points: Map source, treatment, storage and distribution.
Identify customers and critical dependencies.
Check diagrams through a site walk.

activity.prompt: Your drawing omits an emergency bypass. What should the team do?
options: Verify its operation and update the system description.
Ignore it because it is normally closed.
Remove it from the drawing without inspecting it.
activity.feedback: An unusual route may bypass a barrier; establish its actual use and controls.

lessons.example: A small town uses a stream intake most of the year and a bore during dry weather. The diagram shows both sources entering the same tank, but a site walk reveals a bore bypass connected downstream of filtration. Ask which hazards and operating instructions depend on the assumption that all water passes through the filter. Which operating state would make the missing route important?

lessons.title: Hazards and events
lessons.intro: A hazard is something capable of causing harm; a hazardous event allows that hazard to enter or persist. Keeping these separate helps teams select controls that interrupt real contamination pathways. For each stage, describe an event with a cause and route: for example, animals entering an intake enclosure or contaminated water entering through a damaged hatch. Then identify who might be exposed. This approach gives the team something concrete to inspect, prevent or monitor.
points: Name the contaminant or organism.
Describe the event and entry route.
Consider normal and abnormal conditions.

activity.prompt: Which statement best describes a hazardous event?
options: Floodwater enters an unsealed wellhead.
A bacterium exists somewhere in nature.
A supplier owns a river intake.
activity.feedback: The event identifies how contamination can reach the supply.

lessons.example: An operator writes “bacteria” on the risk register. A colleague asks how bacteria could enter the reservoir. Together they identify a loose hatch that admits runoff after storms. Compare the usefulness of the original entry with an event statement that names the contaminant, entry route, weather condition and affected asset. Which inspection would directly address the entry route?

lessons.title: Controls and risk
lessons.intro: Risk assessment connects consequences, likelihood and control performance. Record assumptions and uncertainty explicitly so a tidy risk score does not hide weak evidence about an important treatment or protection barrier. A claimed control should have evidence of capability and evidence that it is being operated correctly. Consider whether two barriers rely on the same power supply or person. Where evidence is incomplete, keep the uncertainty visible rather than using a low score to imply confidence.
points: Evaluate existing control effectiveness.
Record residual risk and assumptions.
Prioritise justified improvements.

activity.prompt: A filter is listed as a control but lacks performance evidence. What next?
options: Seek evidence of its capability and operation.
Assume every filter removes every hazard.
Reduce the risk score because a filter is installed.
activity.feedback: An installed asset is not evidence that the hazard is controlled.

lessons.example: A supplier lists a UV unit as its main microbial control. Maintenance records show that the lamp turns on, but the team cannot find the validated flow and water-quality conditions. Discuss what these records establish, what they do not establish, and which evidence would be needed before relying on the control. Would changing raw-water quality alter the capability assessment?

lessons.title: Monitor and respond
lessons.intro: A control needs a practical monitoring method and a response when conditions deteriorate. The person on shift should understand the trigger, their authority and how to obtain help without avoidable delay. Connect each important measurement to a decision the operator can actually make. Include how an observation is recorded and what happens if a sensor or communication link fails. A monitoring plan is incomplete if it describes data collection but leaves an abnormal result without an owner.
points: Specify what, where and how to monitor.
Assign response responsibilities.
Use suitable operational limits and escalation.

activity.prompt: An important control moves outside its approved operating envelope. What next?
options: Apply the approved response and escalate promptly.
Wait for the next annual review.
Delete the reading to prevent confusion.
activity.feedback: Monitoring protects consumers only when abnormal findings lead to action.

lessons.example: An online turbidity alarm sends an email to a former employee. The instrument records a process change overnight, but nobody acts until the following morning. Trace the complete monitoring chain from measurement to acknowledgement and corrective action. Identify which part failed even though the sensor itself was functioning. Where should acknowledgement and escalation be recorded?

lessons.title: Implement and verify
lessons.intro: Implementation is demonstrated through records and observed practice, not only a signed plan. Verification brings together monitoring, inspection and review to test whether the overall approach is protecting consumers in practice. Look for the links between the plan and maintenance schedules, laboratory arrangements, training and incident records. Ask staff to explain a procedure in their own words. A discrepancy may indicate an outdated plan, an impractical instruction or an operating gap; each needs a different correction.
points: Train staff using real procedures.
Keep accessible records and contacts.
Verify the plan works in practice.

activity.prompt: A plan says an alarm is tested, but no one can demonstrate it. What is needed?
options: Check the process and obtain reliable evidence.
Accept the statement as proof.
Replace the whole plan with an alarm screenshot.
activity.feedback: Verification should connect written commitments to demonstrated performance.

lessons.example: A reservoir inspection checklist is signed every month, but staff say the roof cannot be viewed safely using the available access equipment. Rather than assume the signatures prove an effective inspection, explore how the work is actually done and what safe arrangement would provide evidence about the asset condition. How could the inspection be made both safe and effective?

lessons.title: Review and improve
lessons.intro: Plans need review after meaningful changes, incidents and new knowledge. Improvements work best when an owner, resources and completion evidence are identified, with interim controls for risks that cannot be removed immediately. Review should be triggered by the meaning of a change, not only a calendar reminder. New catchment activities, repeated alarms and changed responsibilities can all alter assumptions. Close an improvement only when its intended effect is demonstrated and affected instructions, training and asset records agree.
points: Review after incidents and changes.
Assign improvement owners and deadlines.
Check completed changes reduce risk.

activity.prompt: An intake is relocated. Which is the best planning response?
options: Review hazards, controls and the supply description before routine use.
Keep the original risk assessment unchanged.
Update only the cover photograph.
activity.feedback: A different location can change both source risks and treatment demands.

lessons.example: Following a flood, the team raises a vulnerable electrical cabinet and marks the action complete. A review finds that the alarm transmitter still uses a low-mounted power connection. Discuss why the original improvement did not fully address the shared vulnerability and what evidence should support final closure. Which other components might share the same flood exposure?

questions.question: Why walk the actual supply route before finalising a plan?
options: To check the drawing against real assets and water pathways
To avoid consulting operators
To replace every maintenance inspection
questions.explanation: An old drawing can miss a bypass or connection. A site walk helps reveal where water actually travels and which controls it encounters. A useful system description follows actual water routes, dependencies and operating modes. Drawings need checking against what staff find on site, including bypasses, seasonal sources and unusual operating arrangements.

questions.question: Who should contribute practical operational knowledge to a planning team?
options: Only the designer of the plan cover
Only staff who have never visited the supply
People familiar with day-to-day operation and relevant specialist risks
questions.explanation: Operators can explain unusual modes, recurring faults and undocumented workarounds. Specialist input complements that knowledge where expertise is needed rather than replacing practical supply understanding. A useful system description follows actual water routes, dependencies and operating modes. Drawings need checking against what staff find on site, including bypasses, seasonal sources and unusual operating arrangements.

questions.question: Why identify critical customers in the system description?
options: Their presence removes monitoring duties
Their needs affect continuity and communication planning
They automatically receive higher-quality treatment
questions.explanation: Hospitals and other sensitive users may have particular continuity needs. Identifying them supports realistic emergency arrangements and communication without assuming a different legal water-quality standard. A useful system description follows actual water routes, dependencies and operating modes. Drawings need checking against what staff find on site, including bypasses, seasonal sources and unusual operating arrangements.

questions.question: What should an emergency-only source contribute to a system description?
options: Its connection, use conditions, risks and safeguards
Only its name because it is rarely used
Nothing until it is needed in an emergency
questions.explanation: An emergency connection may introduce unfamiliar source hazards. Describing it in advance helps operators avoid making critical decisions during an interruption without understanding the water route. A useful system description follows actual water routes, dependencies and operating modes. Drawings need checking against what staff find on site, including bypasses, seasonal sources and unusual operating arrangements.

questions.question: Why record power and communications dependencies?
options: They determine whether bacteria exist in water
They replace the need to describe pipework
Their failure can interrupt treatment, monitoring or response
questions.explanation: A supply may rely on electricity for dosing and telemetry for alarms. Dependency mapping identifies how apparently external failures could affect safe operation or timely intervention. A useful system description follows actual water routes, dependencies and operating modes. Drawings need checking against what staff find on site, including bypasses, seasonal sources and unusual operating arrangements.

questions.question: Which pairing distinguishes hazard from hazardous event?
options: An operator; every routine maintenance visit
Faecal pathogens; runoff entering a damaged wellhead
Flooding; the colour of the plan
questions.explanation: Pathogens are the harmful agents in this example. The runoff entry event explains how they reach the water and points toward protection measures and inspection needs. A hazard is something capable of causing harm; a hazardous event allows that hazard to enter or persist. Keeping these separate helps teams select controls that interrupt real contamination pathways.

questions.question: Why examine conditions after heavy rain?
options: Runoff and source conditions may create different contamination pathways
Rain always improves all source water quality
Only annual average rainfall affects water safety
questions.explanation: Event conditions can challenge an intake differently from routine dry weather. Consider where contaminants may come from and whether existing barriers remain appropriate during that change. A hazard is something capable of causing harm; a hazardous event allows that hazard to enter or persist. Keeping these separate helps teams select controls that interrupt real contamination pathways.

questions.question: Why consider a cross-connection in a distribution risk assessment?
options: It necessarily improves disinfectant performance
It is relevant only to road traffic
It may provide a route from another system into drinking water
questions.explanation: A connection to a lower-quality water system can create a contamination pathway under certain pressure conditions. Identify connections and suitable protective measures using competent local assessment. A hazard is something capable of causing harm; a hazardous event allows that hazard to enter or persist. Keeping these separate helps teams select controls that interrupt real contamination pathways.

questions.question: What is an appropriate way to use complaint information?
options: Exclude complaints because they are not laboratory data
Investigate patterns alongside operational and sampling evidence
Treat every complaint as a confirmed pathogen result
questions.explanation: Complaints can identify changes in taste, odour or pressure. They are useful intelligence but need investigation and context before drawing conclusions about contamination or its cause. A hazard is something capable of causing harm; a hazardous event allows that hazard to enter or persist. Keeping these separate helps teams select controls that interrupt real contamination pathways.

questions.question: Why distinguish a hazard from its source?
options: Controls may target entry pathways as well as the harmful agent
Every source has one fixed hazard forever
The distinction removes the need for sampling
questions.explanation: A catchment activity is a potential origin, while a hazard is the harmful agent. Identifying both helps connect the activity, transport route and appropriate preventive control. A hazard is something capable of causing harm; a hazardous event allows that hazard to enter or persist. Keeping these separate helps teams select controls that interrupt real contamination pathways.

questions.question: What supports confidence in a listed treatment control?
options: A photograph showing the equipment is new
The size of its purchase invoice
Evidence that it can control the relevant hazard under its operating conditions
questions.explanation: Control capability depends on the hazard and the conditions of use. Seek relevant validation and operating evidence rather than inferring performance from appearance or expense. Risk assessment connects consequences, likelihood and control performance. Record assumptions and uncertainty explicitly so a tidy risk score does not hide weak evidence about an important treatment or protection barrier.

questions.question: How should uncertainty in a risk assessment be handled?
options: Hide uncertainty to keep the score simple
Record it and seek evidence or precautionary controls proportionate to the risk
Treat missing data as proof of low risk
questions.explanation: An uncertain score can give misleading reassurance. Documenting assumptions helps reviewers understand the decision and identify which investigation or interim protection would most improve confidence. Risk assessment connects consequences, likelihood and control performance. Record assumptions and uncertainty explicitly so a tidy risk score does not hide weak evidence about an important treatment or protection barrier.

questions.question: What does residual risk refer to?
options: The risk remaining with the assessed controls in place
The original risk before any control
The financial value of unused treatment chemicals
questions.explanation: Controls may reduce likelihood or consequences without eliminating them. Assessing what remains helps prioritise improvement and avoids assuming that an installed barrier resolves every relevant concern. Risk assessment connects consequences, likelihood and control performance. Record assumptions and uncertainty explicitly so a tidy risk score does not hide weak evidence about an important treatment or protection barrier.

questions.question: Why should improvement priorities consider consequences as well as likelihood?
options: Only frequent events can cause harm
A high consequence automatically proves an event is frequent
An uncommon event can still have serious public-health effects
questions.explanation: Assess the severity and plausible occurrence together using the chosen method. This avoids overlooking a less frequent failure that could affect many consumers or particularly vulnerable people. Risk assessment connects consequences, likelihood and control performance. Record assumptions and uncertainty explicitly so a tidy risk score does not hide weak evidence about an important treatment or protection barrier.

questions.question: When comparing two controls, what is most useful?
options: Which produces the longest report
Their demonstrated suitability and reliability for the identified pathway
Which has the most impressive product name
questions.explanation: A control should interrupt the actual hazard pathway. Compare its capability, dependence on other systems and maintenance needs rather than choosing solely on branding or document volume. Risk assessment connects consequences, likelihood and control performance. Record assumptions and uncertainty explicitly so a tidy risk score does not hide weak evidence about an important treatment or protection barrier.

questions.question: What makes an operational monitoring instruction usable?
options: A defined parameter, method, location, trigger and responsible person
A statement to check water occasionally
A list of equipment without actions
questions.explanation: Monitoring needs enough detail for consistent action by different staff. A defined response connects abnormal observations to the decisions needed to maintain or restore control. A control needs a practical monitoring method and a response when conditions deteriorate. The person on shift should understand the trigger, their authority and how to obtain help without avoidable delay.

questions.question: Why should an alarm have an escalation route?
options: Escalation makes the alarm more accurate
Only managers can notice process changes
The first contact may be unavailable or unable to resolve the event
questions.explanation: An alarm without a workable response chain can leave a deteriorating process unattended. Define backup contacts and authority so action does not depend on a single individual. A control needs a practical monitoring method and a response when conditions deteriorate. The person on shift should understand the trigger, their authority and how to obtain help without avoidable delay.

questions.question: How does operational monitoring differ from final-water verification?
options: It measures every hazard directly
It tracks control performance to support timely process decisions
It always replaces compliance sampling
questions.explanation: An online process measurement may reveal a barrier problem before a laboratory result arrives. Verification serves a complementary purpose and does not make effective operational monitoring optional. A control needs a practical monitoring method and a response when conditions deteriorate. The person on shift should understand the trigger, their authority and how to obtain help without avoidable delay.

questions.question: What should happen when a response procedure cannot safely be performed?
options: Escalate and apply authorised contingency arrangements
Improvise an unapproved chemical dose
Record the task as completed anyway
questions.explanation: Staff should understand the boundaries of their competence and authority. An unworkable procedure is a planning issue that needs escalation rather than undocumented improvisation during a failure. A control needs a practical monitoring method and a response when conditions deteriorate. The person on shift should understand the trigger, their authority and how to obtain help without avoidable delay.

questions.question: Why test an alarm-to-callout chain?
options: To prove source water has no hazards
To replace a treatment performance check
To confirm the notification reaches someone able to act
questions.explanation: A sensor indication alone does not show that a person will receive and respond to a notification. Testing the full chain can reveal failed contacts or communication gaps. A control needs a practical monitoring method and a response when conditions deteriorate. The person on shift should understand the trigger, their authority and how to obtain help without avoidable delay.

questions.question: What is stronger evidence of implementation than a signed cover page?
options: A statement that everyone has read it
Current records and observed use of the planned controls
The number of pages in the plan
questions.explanation: A signed document can authorise a plan but cannot show daily performance. Look for evidence that staff follow procedures, monitor controls and act when conditions depart from expectations. Implementation is demonstrated through records and observed practice, not only a signed plan. Verification brings together monitoring, inspection and review to test whether the overall approach is protecting consumers in practice.

questions.question: What is an appropriate role for internal review?
options: Check whether commitments and records match actual practice
Guarantee that no incident can occur
Replace all external regulatory responsibilities
questions.explanation: Review can uncover gaps between planned actions and operations. It supports improvement but does not provide an absolute safety guarantee or remove obligations that apply to the supplier. Implementation is demonstrated through records and observed practice, not only a signed plan. Verification brings together monitoring, inspection and review to test whether the overall approach is protecting consumers in practice.

questions.question: Why preserve incident records?
options: They prove every incident had the same cause
They are useful only for website publicity
They support investigation, accountability and future learning
questions.explanation: A reliable timeline of conditions, decisions and actions helps teams understand what happened. Retaining original evidence also supports checking whether corrective actions address the actual cause. Implementation is demonstrated through records and observed practice, not only a signed plan. Verification brings together monitoring, inspection and review to test whether the overall approach is protecting consumers in practice.

questions.question: What should staff training demonstrate?
options: Memorisation of a plan filename
Understanding and ability to carry out relevant authorised procedures
Only attendance at a presentation
questions.explanation: Attendance is not the same as practical ability. Discussion, demonstration and supervised tasks help identify whether people can recognise abnormal conditions and perform the role assigned to them. Implementation is demonstrated through records and observed practice, not only a signed plan. Verification brings together monitoring, inspection and review to test whether the overall approach is protecting consumers in practice.

questions.question: Why check that the current plan is accessible on shift?
options: Staff may need instructions and contacts during an abnormal event
Accessibility eliminates the need to train people
Only the newest employee needs a copy
questions.explanation: The right procedure has limited value if it cannot be found when needed. Access arrangements should consider power, network availability and staff working away from the main office. Implementation is demonstrated through records and observed practice, not only a signed plan. Verification brings together monitoring, inspection and review to test whether the overall approach is protecting consumers in practice.

questions.question: Which change should trigger review of relevant plan assumptions?
options: A change in the plan cover colour only
A different font in a meeting agenda
A new source or treatment process
questions.explanation: A material supply change can alter hazards, operating conditions and staff responsibilities. Review relevant assessments before relying on controls that were justified for the previous arrangement. Plans need review after meaningful changes, incidents and new knowledge. Improvements work best when an owner, resources and completion evidence are identified, with interim controls for risks that cannot be removed immediately.

questions.question: What makes an improvement action accountable?
options: A high-level goal without an owner
A named owner, target date, resources and completion evidence
The instruction to improve things soon
questions.explanation: Specific responsibilities and evidence make progress reviewable. Where completion will take time, identify interim controls and explain how the remaining risk is being managed. Plans need review after meaningful changes, incidents and new knowledge. Improvements work best when an owner, resources and completion evidence are identified, with interim controls for risks that cannot be removed immediately.

questions.question: Why review an incident after service is restored?
options: To identify causes and prevent recurrence
To prove the original risk assessment was perfect

lessons.title: Know the measurement

lessons.title: Calibration and verification
lessons.intro: Calibration establishes a relationship between instrument indications and reference values; it is not the same as adjustment. lessons.title: References and traceability

courses.title: Cyanobacteria

lessons.title: Organisms and exposure
lessons.intro: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic microorganisms; some populations can produce toxins. Their presence, abundance and toxin production can vary, so neither water colour nor a single observation reliably establishes the health risk at an intake. Cells can contain toxins, and toxins may also occur dissolved outside the cells. Their distribution and persistence need not be identical. Identify whether the concern involves the raw source, treated water or recreation, because the relevant exposure route and protective response can differ substantially.

Consider drinking-water exposure pathways.

A caller asks whether the whole water supply is unsafe. Separate the observation from the questions about intake conditions, toxins, treatment performance and exposure that would need evidence. Which evidence would relate most directly to drinking-water exposure?

lessons.title: Conditions and catchments
lessons.intro: Bloom risk depends on a combination of source conditions, including nutrients, light, temperature and water movement. Local history and catchment pressures help identify where surveillance and preventive management should be focused before visible problems develop. Use local patterns to plan surveillance while recognising that a new season, altered abstraction or unusual weather can challenge the historical picture.

lessons.title: Surveillance and sampling
lessons.intro: A monitoring programme should account for patchy distributions, changing wind conditions and relevant intake depths. Laboratory advice helps distinguish questions about organism abundance, identity and toxin concentrations so sampling and analysis address the actual decision. lessons.title: Treatment decisions
lessons.intro: Intact cells and dissolved toxins need different treatment considerations. Examine multiple lines of evidence and preserve the timeline so investigators can distinguish plausible causes and identify controls that prevent recurrence.

questions.question: Is one clear follow-up result always sufficient to close an incident?
options: Yes; it guarantees every part of the network is safe
Yes; no operating evidence is needed
No; apply relevant recovery criteria and address the cause
questions.explanation: Recovery is a reasoned decision using applicable requirements and control evidence. A single result cannot automatically resolve continuing vulnerabilities. Recovery should be based on the relevant response criteria and evidence that the contamination pathway and control failures have been addressed. One improved result cannot automatically explain the original detection or demonstrate that every part of the supply is protected.

questions.question: Why verify corrective actions after repairs?
options: To avoid keeping repair records
To establish that the intended protection has been restored
Because an invoice proves microbial safety
questions.explanation: A completed repair needs relevant inspection, operational or sampling evidence under the procedure. Confirming its effect supports a defensible recovery decision. Recovery should be based on the relevant response criteria and evidence that the contamination pathway and control failures have been addressed. One improved result cannot automatically explain the original detection or demonstrate that every part of the supply is protected.

questions.question: What should a post-incident review preserve?
options: The timeline, findings, decisions and improvement actions
Only the final clear sample
Only the title of the incident
questions.explanation: The full record helps identify causes, evaluate the response and prevent recurrence. Keep evidence that explains both the concern and its resolution. Recovery should be based on the relevant response criteria and evidence that the contamination pathway and control failures have been addressed. One improved result cannot automatically explain the original detection or demonstrate that every part of the supply is protected.

questions.question: Why update the safety plan after a new contamination pathway is found?
options: The original document must never change
Updating the date alone eliminates the pathway
The plan should reflect newly understood risks and controls
questions.explanation: Learning becomes useful when it changes risk assessment, procedures or physical controls. Assign follow-up actions and verify their completion. Recovery should be based on the relevant response criteria and evidence that the contamination pathway and control failures have been addressed. One improved result cannot automatically explain the original detection or demonstrate that every part of the supply is protected.

questions.question: What is a careful way to communicate recovery?
options: Suppress uncertainty about unresolved issues
Explain the authorised status and actions using the agreed evidence
Promise that contamination can never happen again
questions.explanation: Clear recovery communication reflects the decision actually made. Avoid absolute guarantees and maintain appropriate advice for any remaining restrictions or monitoring needs. Recovery should be based on the relevant response criteria and evidence that the contamination pathway and control failures have been addressed. One improved result cannot automatically explain the original detection or demonstrate that every part of the supply is protected.

courses.title: Risk and resilience
courses.description: Explore dependencies, disruption scenarios and practical preparation for safe service and recovery.

lessons.title: Risk and service outcomes
lessons.intro: Risk assessment considers what could happen and its consequences; resilience also asks how a supply can prepare, withstand disruption, recover and learn. Define the service outcomes that matter before comparing equipment or improvement proposals. A project can improve normal reliability while offering little help during a regional emergency. Assess what happens to safe service during the event and how restoration would occur afterward. This makes it possible to compare prevention, redundancy, operational flexibility and recovery arrangements against meaningful outcomes.
points: Identify safety and continuity outcomes.
Distinguish hazards from vulnerabilities.
Consider recovery as well as prevention.

activity.prompt: A project prevents one failure but makes recovery harder. What should be assessed?
options: Both the avoided risk and the changed recovery capability.
Only the purchase price.
Only whether the equipment is new.
activity.feedback: Resilience looks beyond one normal operating condition to performance during disruption.

lessons.example: A supplier can buy a larger pump or improve access and spare-part arrangements for its existing station. Neither option is automatically best. Compare the failure scenarios each addresses, its effect on service duration and the assumptions about staff, power and repairs that would determine the actual benefit. How would either option perform during a regional outage?

lessons.title: Dependencies and cascades
lessons.intro: A water supply depends on people, electricity, communications, access and materials as well as treatment assets. A single event can affect several dependencies at once, so an apparently independent backup may share the same underlying vulnerability. Trace each essential function to the resources it needs, then ask whether one event can remove several resources simultaneously. Consider regional competition for fuel, technicians and water carriers. A backup has limited value if it is inaccessible, incompatible or dependent on the same damaged infrastructure.
points: Map essential dependencies.
Look for common-cause failure.
Check backup assumptions under real events.

activity.prompt: Two pumps use one flood-prone electrical cabinet. What is the concern?
options: A common failure can disable both pumps.
Two pumps remove every outage risk.
Electrical location is unrelated to service.
activity.feedback: Redundancy is weaker when components share an unprotected dependency.

lessons.example: A plant has two pumps and a portable generator stored beside the switchboard. Floodwater enters the building and affects all three. Draw the shared dependency in words, then identify what further assessment would be needed before describing a relocated or differently protected backup as independent protection. Could the relocated backup still share a vulnerable access route?

lessons.title: Climate and scenarios
lessons.intro: Past experience is valuable but cannot describe every future condition. Scenario planning examines plausible changes in source quality, availability and access, including compound events, so a team can test assumptions before an actual disruption occurs. Consider how water quality, quantity and treatment demands can change together. Scenario planning is a structured test of assumptions rather than a prediction that one exact future will occur. Include credible compound stresses and make clear which proposed controls depend on resources that may also be constrained.
points: Explore drought, flood and heat scenarios.
Consider compound and cascading events.
Make assumptions and uncertainties explicit.

activity.prompt: A drought plan assumes unlimited alternative supply. What next?
options: Verify availability, quality and delivery during the same drought.
Treat the assumption as a guaranteed control.
Remove alternative supply from discussion.
activity.feedback: An alternative may face the same event and needs its own assessment.

lessons.example: A prolonged dry period increases demand while reducing source availability. The emergency plan relies on carriers, but neighbouring communities are requesting the same service. Discuss why a plan based only on average daily demand would overlook the shared shortage and which assumptions about quantity, quality and delivery need testing. Which other sources might face the same regional drought?

lessons.title: Preparedness and contingencies
lessons.intro: Preparedness turns an emergency concept into practical arrangements that people can use. Equipment, supplier contacts, permissions and procedures need testing against realistic conditions, especially when normal power, access or communication services are unavailable. A contingency should identify its activation conditions, available resources and limits. Check whether the people expected to use it have access, competence and authority. Where a test would affect live operations, plan a safe, controlled method so preparedness work does not itself create an unassessed service risk.
points: Define roles and escalation.
Prepare feasible alternative operations.
Test equipment and arrangements safely.

activity.prompt: A generator is available but the connection has never been checked. What helps?
options: A competent safe test of connection and operating requirements.
Assuming any generator fits any plant.
Waiting for a blackout to discover requirements.
activity.feedback: Preparedness includes compatibility, capacity, safe use and supporting resources.

lessons.example: A generator exercise confirms that the engine starts, but nobody checks the plant connection or load requirements. Later, the exercise report claims the whole plant can operate during an outage. Distinguish what was actually demonstrated from the additional compatibility, capacity and support evidence needed to justify that claim. What controlled test would safely evaluate the missing capability?

lessons.title: Respond and recover
lessons.intro: A response should protect people while managing the disruption and preserving information for recovery decisions. Restoring flow is not the same as establishing that drinking-water quality and protective barriers are satisfactory for the affected supply. Recovery may require staged restoration, inspection and water-quality checks, not just restarting equipment. Keep a record of where conditions changed and who authorised each step. Consumers and critical users need coordinated information about restrictions, service status and the evidence supporting changes to advice.
points: Use authorised incident control.
Assess water safety during restoration.
Document decisions and communicate clearly.

activity.prompt: Water pressure returns after repairs. What else is needed?
options: Apply the relevant water-quality and recovery checks.
Declare full safety based only on pressure.
Discard the repair and sampling records.
activity.feedback: Continuity and safety are related but distinct recovery outcomes.

lessons.example: After a damaged main is repaired, pressure is restored across the area. The team still needs to follow its procedures for water-quality assurance and customer advice. Explain why pressure recovery is an important milestone but cannot alone establish that all relevant contamination concerns and protective requirements have been resolved. Which instructions apply before changing the advice to consumers?

lessons.title: Exercise and improve
lessons.intro: Exercises reveal practical gaps without waiting for an actual emergency. Use a manageable scenario, observe decisions and communication, and turn findings into assigned improvements; later check whether those changes have strengthened performance rather than only updated documents. Choose exercise objectives that can be observed, such as locating a current contact or deciding who can isolate an asset. Record what actually happens rather than what participants say should happen. A later focused retest can establish whether corrected arrangements work when the same constraint is introduced.
points: Run focused tabletop exercises.
Record gaps without blame.
Assign and verify improvements.

activity.prompt: An exercise finds the backup contact list is out of date. What next?
options: Assign correction and verify the revised callout chain.
File the finding without an owner.
Assume staff will remember new numbers.
activity.feedback: An exercise creates value when the gap is actually resolved.

lessons.example: A tabletop exercise removes normal mobile coverage from the scenario. Participants discover that their backup number list is stored only in an online account. Identify the practical gap, assign an improvement and propose a safe retest that would show whether responders can now obtain the information under the same constraint. How will the team establish that the revised arrangement works?

questions.question: How does resilience broaden a supply assessment?
options: It includes preparation, disrupted performance and recovery as well as prevention
It only counts replacement pumps
It guarantees that no failures occur
questions.explanation: A resilient approach considers the whole disruption cycle. Avoid treating the presence of spare equipment as a complete measure of capability. Risk assessment considers what could happen and its consequences; resilience also asks how a supply can prepare, withstand disruption, recover and learn. Define the service outcomes that matter before comparing equipment or improvement proposals.

questions.question: Why define essential service outcomes before choosing upgrades?
options: Every upgrade solves every service problem
The most expensive asset is automatically best
Different proposals may support different safety and continuity needs
questions.explanation: Clear outcomes help compare how options protect consumers and restore service. They also expose trade-offs hidden by a purely equipment-focused discussion. Risk assessment considers what could happen and its consequences; resilience also asks how a supply can prepare, withstand disruption, recover and learn. Define the service outcomes that matter before comparing equipment or improvement proposals.

questions.question: What is a vulnerability in a supply?
options: A record of annual water use
A weakness that makes the supply susceptible to a disruptive event
The event itself in every case
questions.explanation: A flood is an event; unprotected critical equipment in its path is a vulnerability. The distinction helps select practical risk-reduction measures. Risk assessment considers what could happen and its consequences; resilience also asks how a supply can prepare, withstand disruption, recover and learn. Define the service outcomes that matter before comparing equipment or improvement proposals.

questions.question: Why consider recovery time in planning?
options: A prolonged interruption can have important consequences even after damage stops
Only the initial failure matters
Recovery time directly measures pathogen concentration
questions.explanation: Assessment should address how long essential functions may be impaired and what resources restoration needs. Duration can shape both continuity and safety implications. Risk assessment considers what could happen and its consequences; resilience also asks how a supply can prepare, withstand disruption, recover and learn. Define the service outcomes that matter before comparing equipment or improvement proposals.

questions.question: What is a limitation of relying on a single risk score?
options: A score always describes every possible future event
Scores make discussion unnecessary
It can hide assumptions, uncertainty or recovery weaknesses
questions.explanation: Use a score as part of a transparent assessment. Retain the reasoning and evidence so decision-makers understand what the number does and does not represent. Risk assessment considers what could happen and its consequences; resilience also asks how a supply can prepare, withstand disruption, recover and learn. Define the service outcomes that matter before comparing equipment or improvement proposals.

questions.question: Which is a shared dependency for two electrically driven pumps?
options: Their separate painted labels
Their common power supply
Their different serial numbers
questions.explanation: Two assets may fail together when both rely on one vulnerable service. Identify these shared links before claiming that equipment duplication provides independence. A water supply depends on people, electricity, communications, access and materials as well as treatment assets. A single event can affect several dependencies at once, so an apparently independent backup may share the same underlying vulnerability.

questions.question: Why include staff availability in dependency mapping?
options: Safe operation and response depend on people with relevant capability
Only physical assets affect water service
Any person can operate every process without guidance
questions.explanation: Illness, isolation or competing duties can reduce response capacity. Planning should consider competent coverage, handovers and realistic backup arrangements. A water supply depends on people, electricity, communications, access and materials as well as treatment assets. A single event can affect several dependencies at once, so an apparently independent backup may share the same underlying vulnerability.

questions.question: What is a common-cause failure?
options: Any two unrelated faults in different years
An alarm sounding on one healthy pump
One event disabling several protective or backup arrangements
questions.explanation: A shared cause can defeat apparent redundancy. Consider whether flood, fire, power loss or another event could affect multiple resources at once. A water supply depends on people, electricity, communications, access and materials as well as treatment assets. A single event can affect several dependencies at once, so an apparently independent backup may share the same underlying vulnerability.

questions.question: Why assess road access during a flood scenario?
options: Supplies are always delivered regardless of access
Fuel, chemicals, staff and repair materials may not reach the site
Road conditions directly measure treatment dose
questions.explanation: A plant may remain intact but become difficult to support. Dependencies outside the site boundary can determine how long safe operation continues. A water supply depends on people, electricity, communications, access and materials as well as treatment assets. A single event can affect several dependencies at once, so an apparently independent backup may share the same underlying vulnerability.

questions.question: Why check communications as part of an alarm system?
options: A detected failure may not reach responders if communication fails
A sensor alarm can physically repair a pump
Telemetry always operates independently of power
questions.explanation: Detection and response depend on the whole chain. Consider local indications, remote notification and feasible fallback communication under the disruption scenario. A water supply depends on people, electricity, communications, access and materials as well as treatment assets. A single event can affect several dependencies at once, so an apparently independent backup may share the same underlying vulnerability.

questions.question: Why consider future climate variability as well as historical events?
options: Past information is always useless
Future conditions can be predicted with complete certainty
Source conditions and disruptive patterns may change
questions.explanation: History informs planning but should not bound every assumption. Explore plausible changes and document uncertainty rather than relying on a single forecast. Past experience is valuable but cannot describe every future condition. Scenario planning examines plausible changes in source quality, availability and access, including compound events, so a team can test assumptions before an actual disruption occurs.

questions.question: What is a compound-event scenario?
options: Every routine meter reading
A combination such as drought, heat and increased demand affecting the supply together
A single spelling error in a procedure
questions.explanation: Combined stresses can exceed the assumptions used for separate events. Testing them can expose limitations in source capacity, treatment or response resources. Past experience is valuable but cannot describe every future condition. Scenario planning examines plausible changes in source quality, availability and access, including compound events, so a team can test assumptions before an actual disruption occurs.

questions.question: Why assess alternative supplies during the same regional event?
options: They may share the original supply’s constraints
Alternative supplies never require quality checks
A separate business name proves independence
questions.explanation: An alternative source or carrier can also face drought, access or demand problems. Verify feasibility under the conditions in which it would be needed. Past experience is valuable but cannot describe every future condition. Scenario planning examines plausible changes in source quality, availability and access, including compound events, so a team can test assumptions before an actual disruption occurs.

questions.question: What is useful about a scenario with explicit assumptions?
options: It guarantees the scenario will occur
It removes the need to update plans
The team can challenge dependencies and identify missing evidence
questions.explanation: Transparent assumptions make the exercise reviewable. They also help distinguish a confirmed capability from an optimistic statement that still requires testing. Past experience is valuable but cannot describe every future condition. Scenario planning examines plausible changes in source quality, availability and access, including compound events, so a team can test assumptions before an actual disruption occurs.

questions.question: Why consider drought effects on water quality as well as quantity?
options: Lower volume always means fewer contaminants
Changed source conditions can affect treatment challenges and exposure
Drought affects only billing
questions.explanation: Source availability and quality can change together. A continuity plan should not introduce unsafe water or operate treatment outside its assessed capability. Past experience is valuable but cannot describe every future condition. Scenario planning examines plausible changes in source quality, availability and access, including compound events, so a team can test assumptions before an actual disruption occurs.

questions.question: What should a backup generator arrangement demonstrate?
options: Suitable capacity, safe connection, operating support and realistic endurance
Only that a generator is listed in an asset register
That any generator can run every device
questions.explanation: Backup capability depends on practical integration and resources. Competent testing can reveal incompatibility, fuel or start-up issues before an emergency. Preparedness turns an emergency concept into practical arrangements that people can use. Equipment, supplier contacts, permissions and procedures need testing against realistic conditions, especially when normal power, access or communication services are unavailable.

questions.question: Why keep emergency supplier contacts current?
options: A contact list replaces agreements and capability checks
All listed suppliers guarantee immediate delivery
Availability and contact routes can change when rapid help is needed
questions.explanation: Contact information is one part of preparedness. It should be accompanied by realistic understanding of capacity, lead times and event-related constraints. Preparedness turns an emergency concept into practical arrangements that people can use. Equipment, supplier contacts, permissions and procedures need testing against realistic conditions, especially when normal power, access or communication services are unavailable.

questions.question: Why define emergency roles before an event?
options: Only one person should know the whole response
People need clear authority, responsibilities and escalation routes
It means procedures never need adjustment
questions.explanation: Clear roles reduce avoidable delay and conflicting actions. Backup arrangements help preserve response capability if the usual decision-maker is unavailable. Preparedness turns an emergency concept into practical arrangements that people can use. Equipment, supplier contacts, permissions and procedures need testing against realistic conditions, especially when normal power, access or communication services are unavailable.

questions.question: What makes an alternative operating procedure credible?
options: It is assessed, practicable and understood by authorised staff
It exists only as an untested idea
It relies on bypassing every barrier without review
questions.explanation: Contingencies can introduce different risks. Evaluate their safety and feasibility, train relevant staff and identify the conditions under which they may be used. Preparedness turns an emergency concept into practical arrangements that people can use. Equipment, supplier contacts, permissions and procedures need testing against realistic conditions, especially when normal power, access or communication services are unavailable.

questions.question: Why consider local access to essential procedures?
options: Paper copies remove the need for version control
Only office staff ever need instructions
Networks or power may fail when information is needed
questions.explanation: Access plans should support people working under disrupted conditions while ensuring they can identify the current approved instructions and contact information. Preparedness turns an emergency concept into practical arrangements that people can use. Equipment, supplier contacts, permissions and procedures need testing against realistic conditions, especially when normal power, access or communication services are unavailable.

questions.question: What is the first broad priority in a drinking-water disruption?
options: Avoid recording difficult decisions
Protect people while applying the authorised response
Restore normal flow regardless of quality
questions.explanation: Continuity is important, but restoring a potentially unsafe service can create further harm. Response arrangements should address both service and public-health needs. A response should protect people while managing the disruption and preserving information for recovery decisions. Restoring flow is not the same as establishing that drinking-water quality and protective barriers are satisfactory for the affected supply.

questions.question: Why assess water quality during service restoration?
options: Repairs, pressure loss or changed operations can create contamination concerns
Restored flow proves all barriers are working
Only customer appearance complaints matter
questions.explanation: Recovery can involve risks different from normal operation. Apply the relevant procedures and evidence requirements rather than relying on hydraulic recovery alone. A response should protect people while managing the disruption and preserving information for recovery decisions. Restoring flow is not the same as establishing that drinking-water quality and protective barriers are satisfactory for the affected supply.

questions.question: Why maintain a response decision log?
options: It guarantees every choice was correct
It replaces the need to communicate
It records evidence, actions and responsibilities for review
questions.explanation: A contemporaneous log helps coordinate a complex response and preserves the reasoning needed to evaluate outcomes or investigate issues later. A response should protect people while managing the disruption and preserving information for recovery decisions. Restoring flow is not the same as establishing that drinking-water quality and protective barriers are satisfactory for the affected supply.

questions.question: What should updates to consumers provide?
options: Unverified technical claims to reassure people
Relevant status, protective advice and a clear route to further information
An unconditional promise of immediate recovery
questions.explanation: Communication should reflect the current evidence and authorised advice. Explain meaningful changes and avoid unsupported certainty about unresolved safety or restoration issues. A response should protect people while managing the disruption and preserving information for recovery decisions. Restoring flow is not the same as establishing that drinking-water quality and protective barriers are satisfactory for the affected supply.

questions.question: When should contingency arrangements end?
options: When the applicable recovery criteria and authorisations support the change
As soon as the first pump restarts
Whenever social-media attention declines
questions.explanation: Ending a contingency is a decision requiring appropriate evidence. Different functions may recover at different times, so define what normal operation actually requires. A response should protect people while managing the disruption and preserving information for recovery decisions. Restoring flow is not the same as establishing that drinking-water quality and protective barriers are satisfactory for the affected supply.

questions.question: What is a tabletop exercise?
options: An uncontrolled live failure of essential equipment
A substitute for every operational test
A facilitated discussion of roles and decisions in a scenario
questions.explanation: Discussion-based exercises can test understanding and coordination safely. They complement appropriate practical testing rather than demonstrating physical equipment performance by themselves. Exercises reveal practical gaps without waiting for an actual emergency. questions.question: Why include realistic communication constraints in an exercise?
options: They prove communication is less important than assets
They reveal whether response arrangements still work when normal channels fail
They make a scenario automatically impossible
questions.explanation: Testing a plausible constraint helps identify workable fallbacks and contact gaps. The aim is learning about actual capability, not simply completing the exercise. questions.question: What makes an exercise finding actionable?
options: A clear issue, responsible owner and means to verify improvement
A general statement that everyone should be careful
An unassigned list stored without review
questions.explanation: Assigning and checking improvements turns observed gaps into stronger capability. Otherwise the same weakness may remain until a real event. Exercises reveal practical gaps without waiting for an actual emergency. questions.question: Why review a response that appeared successful?
options: Successful responses prove all future events are controlled
Review is needed only when equipment is destroyed
Useful lessons may still emerge about delays, risks or untested assumptions
questions.explanation: Success can depend on luck or individual effort. Review helps distinguish reliable arrangements from fragile workarounds and supports sustainable improvement. questions.question: How can an improvement be shown to strengthen resilience?
options: Assume every purchase produces equal benefit
Demonstrate its effect on the intended service outcome under relevant conditions
Count only the pages added to the plan

courses.title: Source water
courses.description: Trace contamination pathways, investigate changing catchments and build practical source-protection decisions.

sources.title: NZ source water risk management guidance
WHO water safety plan manual, second edition
NZ Ministry guidance: source water risk management areas

lessons.title: Follow the water, not the fence
lessons.intro: A community bore sits inside a tidy fenced compound, yet the water reaching it may have travelled from land well outside that fence. Start a source investigation by describing the water body, abstraction point, surrounding activities and routes by which contaminants could arrive. Surface water, groundwater and roof-collected rainwater present different pathways. A useful map includes uncertainties and connections, rather than giving false confidence through a neat boundary.
points: Distinguish the source water body from the intake equipment.
Map potential pathways as well as nearby activities.
Use technical advice where groundwater boundaries are uncertain.

activity.prompt: Your source map stops at the property fence. What improves it?
options: Extend it using catchment or groundwater pathway evidence.
Add more colours within the existing boundary.
Assume neighbouring land cannot affect the source.
activity.feedback: A property boundary does not define where water or contamination can travel. Seek catchment and hydrogeological evidence.

lessons.example: A rural bore is fenced, but a nearby swale carries runoff toward its headworks after heavy rain. Start with two separate questions: could water enter through a defect at the borehead, and could contaminants reach the aquifer through recharge elsewhere? A fence helps manage access but answers neither question. Add the swale and bore construction information to the investigation, and seek groundwater expertise for pathways below ground.

lessons.title: Find a hazard and its route
lessons.intro: Imagine a fuel store, stock access and a road crossing upstream of an intake. Each is a lead for investigation, not proof that contamination is occurring. Separate the harmful agent from the event that releases it and the route that carries it to water. Then ask whether people could be exposed after existing controls. This chain turns a vague list of nearby land uses into a practical investigation that can guide conversations and evidence collection.
points: A hazard is something with potential to cause harm.
An event can release or mobilise that hazard.
A pathway links the event to the water supply.
Evidence determines the significance of a plausible scenario.

activity.prompt: A new fuel store appears upstream. What is the best first assessment?
options: Investigate storage controls, spill pathways and response contacts.
Declare the water contaminated without evidence.
Ignore it until a customer complains.
activity.feedback: Assess a credible release pathway and existing controls. A potential hazard needs investigation, not an unsupported conclusion.

lessons.example: A workshop upstream stores fuel beside a stormwater drain. Describe the scenario as a spill entering that drain, reaching the stream and challenging the intake. Then investigate containment, drainage connections and how the supplier would learn about a release. This description is more useful than simply listing industry as a hazard: it identifies the event, the route and the people who could interrupt it.

lessons.title: Notice change before it becomes a surprise
lessons.intro: A source is not a fixed-quality input. Rainfall, drought, construction, seasonal land use and changes in abstraction can alter the challenge arriving at treatment. Compare observations with the conditions under which they occurred, rather than treating one good sample as a permanent description. Build an event timeline using rainfall, field observations, raw-water measurements and operational records. The aim is to notice meaningful changes early enough for the responsible team to investigate and use its response arrangements.
points: Link observations to weather and catchment events.
Review unusual trends as well as single results.
Include proposed source changes in review.

activity.prompt: Raw-water turbidity rises after repeated storms. Which response develops understanding?
options: Compare event records, intake observations and treatment performance.
Use the annual average to dismiss the change.
Wait for the next routine annual review.
activity.feedback: A linked timeline helps determine whether the source challenge has changed and whether controls remain adequate.

lessons.example: An operator notices that raw-water turbidity rises earlier in storms than it did last season. A recent earthworks project is one possible explanation, but not a proven cause. Compare rainfall timing, intake observations, instrument checks and the works schedule. The investigation may identify a changed runoff pathway, a measurement issue or several contributing factors. Keep those possibilities separate until the evidence distinguishes them.

lessons.title: Share responsibility without losing ownership
lessons.intro: Source protection often requires people who do not operate the treatment plant. A council may hold monitoring information, a neighbour may know local drainage, and mana whenua may contribute place-based knowledge through agreed engagement. The supplier still needs a clear record of what the information means for its supply. Good collaboration establishes who will provide information, who will act on a concern and how progress will be checked. Respectful relationships are an operational resource, not just a consultation entry.
points: Ask local authorities for relevant catchment information.
Record agreed actions with owners and follow-up.
Engage respectfully with mana whenua and affected communities.
Make escalation and incident contacts practical.

activity.prompt: A council agrees to investigate a drainage concern. What belongs in your action log?
options: An owner, agreed task, review date and evidence of completion.
A note saying someone else is handling everything.
Only the date of the first meeting.
activity.feedback: Shared work still needs explicit accountability and confirmation that the control has been implemented.

lessons.example: The supplier identifies a blocked culvert affecting drainage near an intake, while the road authority controls the culvert. Record the observed pathway, contact the responsible organisation and agree who will inspect it. Keep any temporary supplier controls visible in the meantime. A useful follow-up confirms the drainage outcome, rather than closing the concern simply because an email was sent to another organisation.

lessons.title: Choose controls and test the assumptions
lessons.intro: Consider two proposals: repair a leaking borehead seal or add another routine sample each year. Both may provide value, but they do different jobs. A physical control can interrupt a pathway; monitoring can provide evidence about conditions or whether a control is working. Match each proposed action to a stated hazard and explain why it should reduce risk. Keep uncertain assumptions visible, especially when the preferred measure depends on another organisation or on treatment remaining within its verified capability.
points: Explain how each control interrupts a pathway.
Distinguish preventive controls from monitoring evidence.
Verify that controls are present and effective.
Escalate gaps that cannot be resolved locally.

activity.prompt: A damaged borehead seal permits surface entry. Which action addresses the pathway?
options: Arrange approved repair and verify protection is restored.
Increase paperwork without fixing the seal.
Use one good sample to close the defect.
activity.feedback: Repairing the pathway addresses the hazard mechanism; sampling is supporting evidence, not the physical repair.

lessons.example: A bore inspection finds a damaged seal and the latest sample is satisfactory. The sample describes the sampled conditions; it does not show that the opening will resist the next runoff event. Assess the entry route and arrange the appropriate protective response and repair. The completion record should show the restored seal and relevant checks, making clear what changed physically as well as what the testing showed.

lessons.title: Turn investigation into a living plan
lessons.intro: A source plan earns its value when operators can use it during a difficult shift. Record the current source description, credible hazards, controls, observations and response decisions in language that a new colleague can follow. Link the source assessment to the broader drinking-water safety plan, including what treatment can and cannot manage. Review after changes, incidents and new information.
